law_name: Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012

definitions.law_name: Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012
definitions.definition: A person abets an offence under this Act who instigates any person to do that offence; or engages with one or more persons in any conspiracy for the doing of that offence, if an act or illegal omission takes place in pursuance of that conspiracy; or intentionally aids, by any act or illegal omission, the doing of that offence, including by employing, harbouring, receiving or transporting a child by means of threat, coercion, abduction, fraud, deception, or abuse of power for the purpose of any offence under this Act.
definitions.plain_english: Abetment means helping, encouraging, or assisting someone else to commit a crime against a child under this law. It covers three main ways: pushing or tricking someone into committing the offence, secretly planning the offence with others, or actively helping before or during the offence. Even if you didn't physically commit the act yourself, you can still be held equally responsible if you played any of these supporting roles.
real_world_examples: A school teacher in Mumbai who persuades a relative to gain access to a student and sexually assault the child, by falsely telling the relative the child has no family support, is guilty of abetment through wilful misrepresentation and instigation.

A boarding house warden in Delhi who knowingly provides a private room and covers up the presence of an adult known to sexually exploit children residing there, thereby facilitating the commission of penetrative sexual assault, is liable for abetment by aiding.

A trafficker in West Bengal who recruits a 12-year-old girl from a village by deceiving her parents with false promises of education and then transports her to another city where she is subjected to sexual assault, is guilty of abetment under the trafficking-specific limb of Section 16.

Two neighbours in Chennai who conspire together to lure a child to an isolated location knowing one of them intends to commit sexual assault, and where the assault subsequently occurs, are both liable for abetment by conspiracy.

A parent in Rajasthan who, aware that their employer regularly sexually harasses their child, conceals this material fact from authorities and continues to send the child to work at the employer's premises, thereby procuring continued exposure to the offence, is guilty of abetment by wilful concealment.

A social media contact in Hyderabad who coaches a stranger online on how to gain the trust of a minor and advises on methods to isolate the child before committing sexual assault is liable for abetment by instigation and intentional aid.
what_it_covers: A person who instigates another to commit a sexual offence against a child, including through wilful misrepresentation or deliberate concealment of a material fact they were duty-bound to disclose.
Any person who participates in a prior conspiracy with one or more others to commit an offence under the Act, provided an act or illegal omission is carried out in furtherance of that conspiracy.

A person who intentionally aids the commission of the offence before or at the time it occurs, including by providing a location, facilitating access to the child, or removing obstacles to the commission of the act.

A person who employs, harbours, receives, or transports a child using threat, coercion, abduction, fraud, deception, abuse of power, or financial inducement over a person with control of the child, for the purpose of committing any offence under the Act.
A person who voluntarily causes or procures, or attempts to procure, the commission of the offence through wilful misrepresentation or concealment.
what_it_excludes: A person who had no knowledge of the offence being committed and inadvertently provided assistance without any criminal intent or awareness, as abetment requires intentionality or wilfulness.
Mere presence at the scene of the offence without any act of instigation, conspiracy, or intentional aid, since passive bystander conduct without facilitation does not constitute abetment.

A person who commits the sexual offence directly as the principal perpetrator, as they are charged under the substantive offence provisions and not under the abetment provisions of Sections 16 and 17.

Reporting or disclosure of information about the offence to authorities, even if such disclosure results in a subsequent investigation or action, as this is not instigation or facilitation of the offence itself.

Actions taken under lawful authority, such as a police officer or medical professional handling a case in an official capacity, even if their actions indirectly relate to circumstances surrounding the offence.
definitions.why_it_matters: A person found guilty of abetment under Section 16 is punished under Section 17 with the same punishment prescribed for the principal offence that was abetted, meaning abetment of penetrative sexual assault or aggravated sexual assault attracts the same severe mandatory sentences as direct commission; this definition therefore directly triggers criminal liability and sentencing equivalent to that of the primary offender, and also implicates related obligations such as mandatory reporting where concealment forms the basis of abetment.

definitions.law_name: Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012
definitions.definition: An 'advocate' under the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012 refers to a person enrolled and entitled to practice as an advocate under the Advocates Act, 1961, who has been in such practice. In the context of Section 32, an advocate must have been in practice for not less than seven years to be eligible for appointment as a Special Public Prosecutor under this Act.
definitions.plain_english: An advocate is a trained and licensed legal professional who is enrolled with a Bar Council and is qualified to appear and argue cases in court. Under this law, an advocate becomes particularly important when appointing Special Public Prosecutors — lawyers who are specifically chosen to handle child sexual abuse cases in Special Courts. To qualify for this role, the advocate must have at least seven years of legal practice experience.
real_world_examples: A lawyer enrolled with the Bar Council of Maharashtra since 2010 with over a decade of criminal law practice is considered eligible to be appointed as a Special Public Prosecutor under POCSO in a Mumbai Special Court.

An advocate in Delhi who has been practicing for only three years applies to be a Special Public Prosecutor for a POCSO Special Court but is rejected because she does not meet the minimum seven-year practice requirement under Section 32.

During recording of a child victim's statement before a Magistrate in Chennai under Section 164 CrPC, the Magistrate does not allow the accused's advocate to be present in the room, as permitted by the proviso under Section 25 of POCSO.

The State Government of Karnataka issues a gazette notification appointing an advocate with 12 years of criminal law experience as the Special Public Prosecutor for the designated POCSO Special Court in Bengaluru.

In a POCSO trial in Hyderabad, the accused communicates with his advocate through an intercom system while the child witness testifies behind a screen, ensuring the child is not exposed to the accused as mandated under Section 36.

An advocate who has been practicing exclusively in civil matters for eight years is technically eligible under the seven-year requirement but may be passed over in favour of someone with criminal law experience when the State Government appoints a Special Public Prosecutor.
what_it_covers: A person enrolled with any State Bar Council under the Advocates Act, 1961, who has been in active legal practice for seven or more years and is eligible for appointment as Special Public Prosecutor.
An advocate representing the accused in POCSO proceedings before a Special Court, who is entitled to communicate with the accused even during a child's testimony as provided under Section 36.
A senior criminal lawyer with the requisite experience appointed by a State Government via Official Gazette notification to exclusively conduct POCSO cases in a designated Special Court.
An advocate appearing on behalf of the child victim or the State during proceedings including bail hearings, framing of charges, and trial before the Special Court.
what_it_excludes: A law graduate who has not yet enrolled with a State Bar Council and is not entitled to practice as an advocate, regardless of their academic qualifications.
A legal intern or paralegal assisting a practicing advocate but not themselves enrolled or licensed to independently appear and argue in court.
An advocate with fewer than seven years of practice, who, even if otherwise qualified, cannot be appointed as a Special Public Prosecutor under Section 32 of POCSO.
A retired judge or retired public servant with legal knowledge but who is not enrolled as an advocate under the Advocates Act, 1961.

The presence of the accused's advocate at the time a child's statement is recorded by a Magistrate under Section 164 CrPC, as that right is specifically excluded by the proviso to Section 25 of POCSO.
definitions.why_it_matters: The definition of 'advocate' directly governs the eligibility criteria for appointment as a Special Public Prosecutor under Section 32, and failure to meet the seven-year practice requirement renders an appointment invalid, potentially affecting the entire prosecution of POCSO cases. It also determines the boundaries of the accused's right to legal representation during sensitive proceedings such as recording of a child's testimony, where an advocate's presence may be restricted to protect the child.

definitions.law_name: Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012
definitions.definition: 'Aggravated penetrative sexual assault' has the same meaning as assigned to it in section 5, which enumerates circumstances where penetrative sexual assault is committed by persons in positions of authority or trust (such as police officers, armed forces personnel, public servants, hospital or educational institution staff), or involves aggravating factors such as use of deadly weapons, gang assault, assault causing grievous hurt, pregnancy, HIV infection, death, assault on a child below twelve years, or assault by a relative or person in a domestic relationship with the child.
definitions.plain_english: Aggravated penetrative sexual assault refers to particularly serious forms of child sexual penetration that are made worse by who commits the act or how it is committed. For example, it includes situations where a police officer, teacher, doctor, or family member sexually penetrates a child, or where the assault involves weapons, causes serious injury, results in pregnancy or a deadly disease, or is carried out repeatedly or by a group. Because of these worsening circumstances, the law treats this offence far more severely than ordinary penetrative sexual assault.
real_world_examples: A school principal in Delhi commits penetrative sexual assault on a student within the school premises — this qualifies as aggravated penetrative sexual assault because the accused is on the management or staff of an educational institution.

A police constable in Mumbai, while on duty and in uniform, commits penetrative sexual assault on a minor victim at the police station — this is aggravated penetrative sexual assault because it is committed by a police officer within the limits of the police station.

A group of men in a village in Uttar Pradesh gang-assault a child, where multiple persons commit penetrative sexual assault together — this constitutes aggravated penetrative sexual assault under the gang penetrative sexual assault clause.

A child's uncle, who lives in the same household in Chennai, repeatedly commits penetrative sexual assault on the child over several months — this is aggravated penetrative sexual assault because the perpetrator is a relative living in a shared household and the assault is committed more than once.

A government hospital staff member in Kolkata sexually penetrates a child patient admitted under their care — this constitutes aggravated penetrative sexual assault as the offender is on the management or staff of a hospital.

An army personnel posted in a conflict zone in Manipur commits penetrative sexual assault on a minor within the area of deployment — this qualifies as aggravated penetrative sexual assault as it is committed by a member of the armed forces or security forces in the area to which they are deployed.
semantic_tags: assault causing grievous hurt or death
assault by family member or relative
what_it_covers: Penetrative sexual assault committed by a police officer, armed forces or security forces member, or public servant in the course of their duties or within their jurisdictional premises.
Penetrative sexual assault committed by management or staff of educational institutions, religious institutions, hospitals, or child care and custody establishments on a child in their care.
Gang penetrative sexual assault, where more than one person acts in furtherance of a common intention to commit the offence.
Penetrative sexual assault that causes grievous hurt, bodily harm, injury to sexual organs, pregnancy, infection with HIV or other life-threatening disease, or death of the child.
Penetrative sexual assault on a child below the age of twelve years, or committed repeatedly, or by a relative or person sharing a household with the child.
Penetrative sexual assault involving use of deadly weapons, fire, heated substances, or corrosive substances.
what_it_excludes: Simple penetrative sexual assault not accompanied by any aggravating circumstance enumerated in section 5, which is separately governed by section 3 and section 4.
Sexual assault (non-penetrative) even if committed by a person in a position of authority — such conduct may fall under aggravated sexual assault under section 9 but not under this definition.
Sexual harassment as defined in section 11, which involves non-contact acts and is governed by section 12, not by the penetrative assault provisions.

Penetrative sexual assault committed by a private individual with no position of trust, authority, or domestic relationship with the child, and without any of the additional aggravating factors listed in section 5.
Child pornography offences under section 13 and 14, which may involve children but do not require an act of physical penetrative assault as the defining element.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act qualifies as aggravated penetrative sexual assault under section 5 determines the quantum of punishment: section 6 prescribes a minimum sentence of twenty years' rigorous imprisonment extendable to imprisonment for life and a fine, as opposed to the minimum of ten years under section 4 for ordinary penetrative sexual assault. This classification also triggers heightened presumptions of culpable mental state under section 29 and affects the sentencing framework applied by Special Courts under section 28.

definitions.law_name: Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012
definitions.definition: 'Aggravated sexual assault' has the same meaning as assigned to it in section 9, which provides that a person is said to commit aggravated sexual assault when they commit sexual assault on a child under circumstances that aggravate the gravity of the offence, including where the offender holds a position of authority, trust, or power over the child, or where the act causes severe physical or psychological harm, or where the child is particularly vulnerable by reason of age, disability, or relationship to the offender.
definitions.plain_english: Aggravated sexual assault refers to cases of sexual assault on a child that are considered especially serious because of who committed the act or how it was done. For example, if the person who committed the assault was a police officer, teacher, doctor, or a family member, or if the assault was particularly brutal, repeated, or caused serious injury, it falls into this more severe category. It is treated as worse than ordinary sexual assault because of the extra harm caused or the betrayal of trust involved.
real_world_examples: A government school teacher in Uttar Pradesh sexually assaults a minor student on school premises — the accused being on the staff of an educational institution committing the act within that institution qualifies this as aggravated sexual assault under Section 9.

A constable posted at a police station in Maharashtra sexually assaults a child within the premises of the station house — the act committed by a police officer within police premises constitutes aggravated sexual assault.

A relative (uncle) living in the same shared household as a child in Tamil Nadu repeatedly commits sexual assault on the child — both the familial relationship and the repeated nature of the assault bring this within the definition of aggravated sexual assault.

A doctor employed at a private hospital in Delhi sexually assaults a minor patient admitted for treatment — the accused being on the management or staff of a hospital and committing the act within that hospital constitutes aggravated sexual assault.

During communal riots in a city in Gujarat, a perpetrator sexually assaults a minor child — the act committed during communal or sectarian violence is explicitly recognised as aggravated sexual assault under Section 9.

A person previously convicted of a sexual offence under the POCSO Act commits sexual assault on a child in Kolkata — the prior conviction combined with the fresh offence qualifies the act as aggravated sexual assault.
semantic_tags: child sexual abuse by authority figures
assault by armed forces or police
what_it_covers: Sexual assault committed by a police officer, armed forces personnel, public servant, or government employee on a child in the course of or in relation to their official duties or within official premises.

Sexual assault committed by a person in a position of trust or authority over the child, including relatives by blood, adoption, marriage or guardianship, staff of educational or religious institutions, hospital staff, or persons managing any child care institution.
Sexual assault that causes grievous hurt, bodily harm, injury to sexual organs, physical incapacitation, mental illness, or infliction of life-threatening diseases such as HIV on the child victim.
Sexual assault committed on a child below twelve years of age, on a pregnant child, on a child with mental or physical disability, or on a child with the intent to murder the child.

Gang sexual assault on a child, assault using deadly weapons, fire, heated or corrosive substances, repeated assaults, assaults during communal violence or natural calamities, and assaults by persons previously convicted under POCSO or other sexual offence laws.
what_it_excludes: Sexual assault committed by an ordinary private individual with no special authority, trust, or relationship over the child and without any of the aggravating circumstances listed in Section 9 — such an act constitutes 'sexual assault' under Section 7, not aggravated sexual assault.

Penetrative sexual assault and aggravated penetrative sexual assault, which are separately defined under Sections 3 and 5 respectively and carry distinct and generally higher punishments, are excluded from the scope of this definition.

Sexual harassment of a child as defined under Section 11, which involves non-contact acts such as making sexually coloured remarks or showing pornographic material, falls outside the scope of aggravated sexual assault.
Acts constituting child pornography or use of a child for pornographic purposes, which are governed by separate provisions under the Act and do not by themselves constitute aggravated sexual assault.
Offences committed against adults (persons eighteen years of age or above), which fall outside the jurisdiction of POCSO entirely and are governed by other laws such as the Indian Penal Code.
definitions.why_it_matters: A conviction for aggravated sexual assault under Section 9 attracts a mandatory minimum punishment of five years of imprisonment extendable up to seven years along with a fine under Section 10, which is significantly higher than the punishment for ordinary sexual assault under Section 8. The classification also triggers the presumption of culpability under Section 29, shifts the evidentiary burden to the accused, and engages the enhanced procedural protections and special court mechanisms under Sections 14 and 28 of the Act.

definitions.definition: A fact is said to be proved beyond reasonable doubt only when the Special Court believes it to exist beyond reasonable doubt and not merely when its existence is established by a preponderance of probability. This standard applies specifically in the context of an accused proving the absence of a culpable mental state under Section 30 of the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012.
definitions.plain_english: Beyond reasonable doubt means that the court must be firmly convinced that a fact is true — not just that it is more likely true than not. It is a very high level of certainty, stronger than a mere balance of probabilities. Under POCSO, when an accused tries to prove they had no guilty mental state, they must meet this strict standard of proof.
real_world_examples: An accused charged under POCSO claims he did not know the victim was a child. To successfully use this as a defence, he must place evidence before the Special Court in Mumbai that makes the court firmly convinced — beyond reasonable doubt — that he genuinely had no such knowledge, not merely that it was somewhat probable he did not know.

A school teacher in Delhi accused of sexual assault under POCSO argues he lacked any sexual intent during physical contact with a student. The Special Court must be fully convinced, not just partially persuaded, that the teacher had no culpable mental state before accepting this defence.

A man in Chennai prosecuted under POCSO for sharing child pornography claims he was unaware of the nature of the material. For the court to accept his defence, the evidence he presents must rise to the level of beyond reasonable doubt — a mere possibility or balance of chances is insufficient.

In a Kolkata case, an accused under POCSO argues he believed the person to be an adult. The Special Court will apply the beyond reasonable doubt standard to assess his claim that he had no belief or knowledge that the victim was a child, requiring far more than a probable inference in his favour.

A person prosecuted for abetment of penetrative sexual assault in Hyderabad claims he had no motive or intention to facilitate the act. The Special Court must be firmly satisfied — beyond reasonable doubt — that the accused lacked this culpable mental state before the defence can succeed.
what_it_covers: The standard an accused must meet when attempting to prove absence of culpable mental state such as intention, motive, or knowledge in a POCSO prosecution before the Special Court.
The level of judicial belief required — firm and settled conviction in the mind of the Special Court — before a fact is considered proved under Section 30.
Cases where the accused presents evidence that must go beyond a balance of probabilities or preponderance of evidence, and must instead create firm belief in the court's mind.
what_it_excludes: Proof by mere preponderance of probability, meaning it is not enough for the accused to show that it is more likely than not that he lacked a guilty mind.
The standard does not apply to the prosecution's burden regarding the mental state itself, since Section 30 presumes culpable mental state in favour of the prosecution.
Civil law evidentiary standards or balance of probabilities tests used in non-criminal proceedings, which are lower thresholds and not applicable under Section 30 of POCSO.
Speculative or conjectural claims by the accused that merely raise doubt without placing concrete evidence before the Special Court sufficient to meet this high standard.
definitions.why_it_matters: The beyond reasonable doubt standard under Section 30 determines whether an accused can successfully rebut the statutory presumption of culpable mental state — if the accused fails to meet this standard, the court will treat the guilty mental state as proved, directly impacting conviction for offences such as penetrative sexual assault, sexual assault, and child pornography under POCSO. This effectively raises the bar for the accused's defence and tilts the evidentiary burden in favour of the child victim and the prosecution.

definitions.definition: The term 'care and protection' is not expressly defined in Section 2 of the POCSO Act, 2012; however, as used in Section 5 and contextually throughout the Act, it refers to any institutional arrangement — established by or under any law for the time being in force — wherein a child is placed under the supervision, shelter, or custody of an authority or institution for the child's welfare, safety, rehabilitation, or developmental needs, including observation homes, protection homes, remand homes, and similar facilities recognised under child welfare legislation such as the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015.
definitions.plain_english: Care and protection refers to formal institutional settings where children who are vulnerable, in conflict with the law, or without adequate family support are kept safe and looked after by the state or an authorised body. These include government-run or approved homes, shelters, and observation centres meant to protect children from harm. The phrase is borrowed from child welfare law and signals that the child is under the custody and responsibility of an institution rather than a family.
real_world_examples: A child rescued from a trafficking ring in Mumbai is placed in a Child Care Institution (CCI) run by the Maharashtra government under the Juvenile Justice Act — such a facility constitutes a 'place of care and protection', and any staff member who sexually assaults the child there commits aggravated penetrative sexual assault under Section 5 of POCSO.

A staff member at a government-run observation home in Delhi, where children in conflict with the law are housed pending inquiry, sexually assaults a juvenile resident — the home qualifies as a 'place of care and protection', attracting enhanced punishment under POCSO.

A warden at a Bal Ashram (children's shelter home) in Rajasthan, licensed under the Juvenile Justice Act and housing abandoned children, commits penetrative sexual assault on a child inmate — the Ashram is treated as a place of 'care and protection', making the offence aggravated under Section 5.

A child victim of abuse placed by the Child Welfare Committee in a protection home in Chennai under Section 31 of the Juvenile Justice Act is subsequently assaulted by the home's manager — because the facility is a state-recognised 'care and protection' institution, the offence is categorised as aggravated, carrying a minimum 10-year sentence.

A resident staff member at a special home for girls in Kolkata established under the West Bengal Homes (Regulation) Act assaults a child residing there — this triggers Section 5 of POCSO because the home is a place of 'care and protection' under law.

A child placed in foster care through a Juvenile Justice Board order in Pune is sexually assaulted by the caretaker at a registered foster care facility — the institutional nature of the arrangement brings it within the ambit of 'care and protection' settings covered by Section 5.
what_it_covers: Observation homes established under the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015 where children in conflict with law are temporarily housed.
Protection homes and shelter homes licensed or recognised by the state government for housing children who are abandoned, abused, or without family support.
Child Care Institutions (CCIs) set up under any central or state legislation where children are placed under court or Child Welfare Committee orders.
Remand homes or places of custody where children are kept pending legal proceedings under applicable child welfare or criminal laws.
Any government or government-approved facility specifically established for the safety, rehabilitation, and developmental care of vulnerable children.
what_it_excludes: Informal, non-institutional family care arrangements such as a child living with grandparents or relatives without formal state involvement or legal order.
Private residences where a child may be kept by a guardian without any formal registration or recognition under child welfare legislation.
Educational institutions such as schools and colleges, which are separately and specifically enumerated in Section 5 as distinct categories of aggravated offence locations.
Hospitals, whether government or private, which are expressly treated as a separate category in Section 5 and do not fall under the 'care and protection' institutional label.
Informal community-based childcare or crèche arrangements not established or recognised under any law for the time being in force.

definitions.definition: "child" means any person below the age of eighteen years.
definitions.plain_english: A 'child' under this law is any person who has not yet turned 18 years old. This includes boys, girls, and persons of any gender identity. The moment a person completes 18 years of age, they are no longer considered a child under this Act.
real_world_examples: A 15-year-old girl from Mumbai who is sexually assaulted by a neighbor is a 'child' under POCSO, and the offender will be prosecuted under the Act's provisions regardless of whether she is married.
A 17-year-old boy in Delhi who is coerced into participating in the creation of sexually explicit photographs is a 'child' for the purposes of child pornography offences under Section 13 of the Act.

A 10-year-old girl studying in a government school in Chennai who is subjected to inappropriate touching by a teacher is a 'child', and the teacher's act constitutes 'sexual assault' under Section 7 of the Act.

A 16-year-old boy from a rural village in Rajasthan who is lured online and subjected to sexual harassment via social media messages is a 'child', and the perpetrator is liable under Section 11 of the Act.
A 17-year-old married girl in Bihar who is sexually abused by her husband is still a 'child' under POCSO, and her husband can be prosecuted under the Act irrespective of the marital relationship.

An 8-year-old orphan residing in a child care institution in Kolkata who is subjected to penetrative sexual assault by a staff member is a 'child', attracting the provisions of aggravated penetrative sexual assault under Section 5.
what_it_covers: Any person below 18 years of age, regardless of gender, who is the victim of a sexual offence under the Act.
A married girl below 18 years of age, since Indian law under POCSO does not exclude married minors from the definition of 'child'.

definitions.law_name: Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012
definitions.definition: 'Child pornography' means any visual depiction of sexually explicit conduct involving a child which include photograph, video, digital or computer generated image indistinguishable from an actual child and image created, adapted, or modified, but appear to depict a child.
definitions.plain_english: Child pornography refers to any image or video — whether a real photograph, a recording, or a computer-made picture — that shows a child in a sexually explicit way. This includes not just real photos or videos of actual children, but also digitally created or altered images that look like they involve a child. Even if no real child was directly used to create the image, it still counts as child pornography if it appears to show a child in a sexual situation.
real_world_examples: A person in Mumbai downloads and saves videos depicting minors in sexually explicit acts on their mobile phone — these videos constitute child pornography under the Act.

A Delhi-based graphic designer uses software to create animated or computer-generated images that realistically depict a child engaged in sexual activity — such images fall within the definition even though no real child was involved.
A WhatsApp group in Bengaluru is used to share photographs of children morphed or digitally altered to appear in sexually explicit contexts — these morphed images qualify as child pornography.

A person in Chennai photographs a minor in a sexually explicit manner using a hidden camera and stores the images on a hard drive — those photographs are child pornography and trigger criminal liability under the Act.

An individual in Kolkata creates a short video by editing publicly available footage of a child to make it appear sexually explicit — the modified video falls within the definition of child pornography under POCSO.

A school teacher in Hyderabad possesses a collection of digitally scanned magazine images depicting minors in sexual poses — these scanned images constitute child pornography regardless of the original medium.
what_it_covers: Real photographs taken of an actual child depicting sexually explicit conduct.
Videos — whether recorded or live-streamed — showing a child engaged in or subjected to sexually explicit acts.
Computer-generated or digitally created images that are indistinguishable from images of a real child in sexual contexts.
Photographs or images that have been digitally adapted or morphed to appear to depict a child in a sexually explicit manner, even if the original subject was an adult.
Artificially created images (e.g., deepfakes or animated renderings) that depict a child in sexually explicit situations, regardless of whether any real child was used in their creation.
what_it_excludes: Purely written or textual descriptions of child sexual abuse without any accompanying visual depiction — these do not meet the definition's requirement of a 'visual depiction'.
Audio recordings alone (e.g., voice clips) depicting sexually explicit content involving a child, as the definition is confined to visual material.
Medical or clinical images of children's bodies taken for legitimate diagnostic or treatment purposes by authorised medical professionals, which are not sexually explicit in nature.
Age-appropriate artistic or educational depictions of children (e.g., anatomical diagrams in health textbooks) that do not involve sexually explicit conduct.
Images or videos of adults that are mistakenly believed to depict minors but are objectively and verifiably of persons aged eighteen years or above.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether material qualifies as 'child pornography' under this definition directly determines criminal liability under Section 15 of the Act, which prescribes punishment for storage, possession, transmission, distribution, and commercial exploitation of such material — ranging from fines to imprisonment up to seven years. It also activates the obligation on persons holding such material to delete, destroy, or report it to the designated authority, and failure to do so constitutes a punishable offence.

definitions.law_name: Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012
definitions.definition: The Child Welfare Committee refers to the Committee constituted under Section 27 of the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2000, to which the Special Juvenile Police Unit or local police is required to report, without unnecessary delay and within twenty-four hours, any matter concerning a child against whom an offence under this Act has been committed, including the child's need for care and protection and steps taken in that regard.
definitions.plain_english: The Child Welfare Committee is a government-appointed body responsible for looking after the welfare and safety of children who are victims or in need of protection. When police receive a report of a sexual offence against a child, they must inform this Committee within 24 hours. The Committee then steps in to assess whether the child needs shelter, medical care, or other protective measures.
real_world_examples: In Mumbai, when a local police station receives a complaint that a 10-year-old girl has been sexually assaulted by a neighbour, the police must report the incident to the Child Welfare Committee within 24 hours so it can arrange shelter or counselling for the child.

In rural Rajasthan, after the Special Juvenile Police Unit learns that a 13-year-old boy has been subjected to sexual harassment at a madrasa, they report the matter to the Child Welfare Committee, which then evaluates whether the child should be removed from that environment and placed in a government shelter home.

In Chennai, a hospital social worker reports to the local police that a 7-year-old child brought in for treatment shows signs of sexual abuse. The police immediately inform the Child Welfare Committee, which deploys a case worker to assess the child's home situation and need for protection.

In Delhi, a child helpline worker reports to the Special Juvenile Police Unit that a 15-year-old domestic worker has been sexually exploited by her employer. Within 24 hours, the police notify the Child Welfare Committee, which arranges for the child's transfer to a children's home and initiates rehabilitation proceedings.

In Kolkata, after a teacher reports a suspected case of child sexual abuse at a school, the local police file a report and simultaneously notify the Child Welfare Committee, which arranges for a special educator and counsellor to support the child through the investigation process.
what_it_covers: The statutory committee constituted under the Juvenile Justice Act to which police must report within 24 hours when a child victim of a POCSO offence is identified.

Cases where the Special Juvenile Police Unit or local police determine that a child against whom an offence has been committed is in need of care and protection, triggering a mandatory referral to the Committee.
Situations where the Committee receives information about steps taken by police, including admission of the child to a shelter home or hospital, and oversees further protective action.
Any child who has been the subject of a reported offence under POCSO, regardless of whether a Special Court has been designated, as police must report to the Committee in all such cases.
what_it_excludes: Police stations or law enforcement agencies themselves, which are obligated to report to the Committee but do not form part of it.
The Special Court or Court of Session, which is a separate judicial body to which police also report under Section 19(6) but which performs an adjudicatory rather than welfare function.

Non-governmental organisations or private child welfare bodies, which may assist children but are not the 'Child Welfare Committee' as envisaged under the Juvenile Justice framework referenced in this Act.
Adults or persons above the age of 18, as the Committee's jurisdiction is exclusively over children in need of care and protection.
definitions.why_it_matters: Failure by the Special Juvenile Police Unit or local police to report a case to the Child Welfare Committee within 24 hours constitutes a lapse in the mandatory procedural obligation under Section 19(6), which can result in departmental action and jeopardises timely protective intervention for the child victim. The Committee's involvement directly determines whether a child is placed in emergency shelter, receives medical care, or is brought under the formal child protection system, and its assessment influences subsequent proceedings before the Special Court.

definitions.law_name: Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012
definitions.definition: A 'children's court' means a Court of Session notified as such under the Commissions for Protection of Child Rights Act, 2005 (4 of 2006), or a Special Court designated for similar purposes under any other law for the time being in force, which, by virtue of such notification, shall be deemed to be a Special Court under Section 28 of this Act for the purposes of trying offences under the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012.
definitions.plain_english: A children's court is a regular Sessions Court that has been officially designated by the State Government specifically to handle cases involving children, either under the child rights law or another similar law. When such a court already exists in a district, it automatically becomes the Special Court for handling cases under the POCSO Act as well. This avoids the need to create a separate court and ensures that child-sensitive infrastructure is used efficiently.
real_world_examples: In Delhi, a Court of Session already notified as a children's court under the Commissions for Protection of Child Rights Act, 2005 is automatically treated as the Special Court under POCSO to try a case where a 10-year-old girl was sexually assaulted by a neighbour.

In Maharashtra, the State Government designates a Sessions Court in Pune as a children's court under the CPCR Act; this same court proceeds to hear a POCSO case involving online sexual exploitation of a minor without any fresh notification being required.

In Tamil Nadu, a Special Court for children already functioning under a State child protection law in Chennai is deemed the POCSO Special Court when charges are framed against a school teacher accused of aggravated sexual assault on students.

In Uttar Pradesh, a district where no separate POCSO Special Court exists relies on the existing children's court notified under the CPCR Act in Lucknow to conduct speedy trials for multiple child sexual abuse cases reported in that jurisdiction.

In Karnataka, a children's court in Bengaluru, already handling juvenile matters under child rights legislation, is called upon to try an accused under both POCSO and Section 67B of the Information Technology Act for transmitting sexually explicit material depicting children online.
what_it_covers: A Court of Session notified as a children's court under the Commissions for Protection of Child Rights Act, 2005 (4 of 2006) in any district of a State.
A Special Court designated for purposes similar to child protection under any other law in force, which automatically acquires jurisdiction to try POCSO offences.

Trials under Section 67B of the Information Technology Act, 2000 relating to publication or transmission of sexually explicit material depicting children, when conducted by such a children's court acting as POCSO Special Court.
Cases where the accused faces charges under the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 for connected offences tried alongside the main POCSO offence in the same court.
what_it_excludes: A Magistrate's Court or Judicial Magistrate's court, as only a Court of Session can be designated or deemed a children's court or Special Court under Section 28.

A Juvenile Justice Board constituted under the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, even though it handles child-related matters, as it is not a Court of Session and is not notified as a children's court for POCSO purposes.
A Family Court constituted under the Family Courts Act, 1984, which handles matrimonial and custody disputes and is not designated as a children's court for criminal trial purposes under POCSO.

An ad hoc or informal committee or tribunal set up by an institution or private body to inquire into child abuse complaints, as it lacks the statutory notification required to qualify as a children's court.

definitions.law_name: Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012
definitions.definition: Cognizance, as used in the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012, refers to the formal act of a Special Court taking judicial notice of an offence and assuming jurisdiction to try it, either upon receiving a complaint of facts constituting the offence or upon a police report of such facts, without the accused being committed to it for trial. The date of taking cognizance marks the commencement of the court's active role in the proceedings and triggers statutory timelines for recording evidence and completing the trial.
definitions.plain_english: Cognizance means the moment when the Special Court officially 'takes up' or accepts a case against an accused person and begins the legal process of trial. Think of it as the court formally deciding it will hear and deal with the case. This can happen based on a police report (chargesheet) or a direct complaint filed with the court. Once cognizance is taken, important time limits start running — like completing the recording of a child's evidence within 30 days.
real_world_examples: A Special Court in Mumbai receives a chargesheet (police report) from the Mumbai Police against an accused for penetrative sexual assault of a 10-year-old girl under POCSO. The judge formally takes cognizance of the offence on that date, and from that day the 30-day clock for recording the child's evidence begins to run.

In Delhi, a mother files a direct complaint before the POCSO Special Court alleging sexual harassment of her 8-year-old son by a school teacher. The court examines the complaint, finds it discloses a cognizable offence under POCSO, and takes cognizance — initiating the trial process without waiting for a police committal order.

A Special Court in Chennai takes cognizance of a case involving child pornography under POCSO upon receiving the police final report. The court then sets a deadline of one year from this date for completing the entire trial, as mandated by Section 35.

In Kolkata, a POCSO Special Court notes that while cognizance was taken on 1st January 2023, the child's evidence could not be recorded within 30 days due to the child's hospitalisation. The court records reasons for the delay in writing, as required by Section 35, before proceeding further.

A sessions court designated as a POCSO Special Court in Hyderabad takes cognizance of an aggravated penetrative sexual assault case involving a minor victim after the police file a chargesheet. The cognizance date is recorded and all subsequent procedural timelines, including compensation directions under Section 33, are calculated from this date.
what_it_covers: Taking cognizance upon receipt of a police chargesheet or final report filed under Section 173 CrPC disclosing a POCSO offence against a child.
Taking cognizance upon a direct complaint filed by a parent, guardian, or any person on behalf of the child victim before the Special Court, where the facts disclose a POCSO offence.
The act of cognizance without requiring the accused to be first committed to the Special Court for trial, conferring original trial jurisdiction on the Special Court from the point of cognizance.
The date of cognizance as the reference point for computing the 30-day period within which the child's evidence must be recorded under Section 35.
The date of cognizance as the starting point for the one-year outer limit for completing the entire trial under Section 35.
what_it_excludes: Mere registration of an FIR at a police station, which is a police-level step and does not amount to a court taking cognizance of the offence.
The arrest or remand of an accused by a magistrate for police custody purposes, which does not constitute the Special Court taking cognizance of the POCSO offence for trial purposes.
Preliminary inquiries or pre-cognizance investigations conducted by the Child Welfare Committee or Special Juvenile Police Unit, which occur before any court formally takes up the case.
Cognizance by a regular Magistrate or Sessions Court that has not been designated as a Special Court under POCSO, as the Act vests exclusive cognizance jurisdiction in the designated Special Court.

Administrative or executive actions by the police or designated authority following receipt of a complaint, such as filing an FIR or conducting a medical examination, which precede and are distinct from judicial cognizance.
definitions.why_it_matters: The taking of cognizance is the critical procedural trigger under POCSO that activates mandatory statutory timelines — specifically, the 30-day deadline for recording the child's evidence and the one-year deadline for completing the trial under Section 35 — making delay accountable and requiring recorded justification. Without cognizance being formally taken by the Special Court, these child-protective timelines do not begin, potentially delaying justice for the child victim and affecting the legal validity of subsequent proceedings.

definitions.law_name: Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012
definitions.definition: The Act does not formally define 'commercial purpose,' but as used in Section 15(3), it means the storage or possession of pornographic material involving a child with the intent to derive monetary gain, profit, or any financial benefit from such material, including through sale, subscription, pay-per-view, or any other transaction involving consideration.
definitions.plain_english: Commercial purpose means storing or keeping child sexual abuse material with the goal of making money from it. This includes selling such material, charging people to view it, or using it in any business-like way to earn profit. It does not matter whether the person actually succeeded in making money — the intent to profit is enough to attract this higher level of punishment.
real_world_examples: An operator in Mumbai runs a paid subscription website hosted on foreign servers where users pay a monthly fee to access child pornographic videos stored on his hard drives — this constitutes storage for commercial purpose.

A person in Delhi purchases child sexual abuse images in bulk and sells them to buyers via encrypted messaging apps like Telegram for a per-clip fee, storing the content on his laptop pending each transaction.
A studio owner in Hyderabad stores recorded videos of child abuse with the intention of selling them to a pornographic content distributor network operating across South Asia for a lump sum payment.
A cyber café operator in Chennai stores child pornographic material on the café's server and charges select customers extra fees for private access to such content on designated terminals.
A person in Kolkata accumulates child abuse imagery with the plan to auction it on dark web marketplaces, retaining the material in encrypted folders while soliciting buyers for monetary bids.
what_it_covers: Storing child pornographic material on digital devices with the intent to sell it to buyers for monetary consideration.
Maintaining a paid online platform, server, or cloud storage containing child sexual abuse material accessible to paying subscribers.
Retaining child abuse imagery for distribution to a commercial network or syndicate in exchange for money, cryptocurrency, or any other valuable consideration.
Possessing such material with intent to monetise it through pay-per-view services, dark web auctions, or private sales via encrypted communication channels.
Storing child pornographic content as inventory for a trafficking or exploitation enterprise where the material itself is a traded commodity.
what_it_excludes: Storage of child pornographic material solely for the purpose of reporting it to the designated authority as prescribed under Section 15(1) — which is a protected act under the Act.
Possession of such material retained exclusively as evidence for use in court proceedings, which is explicitly carved out in Section 15(2).

Storage or possession without any profit motive, such as a person who downloads and keeps the material for personal consumption without any intent to sell, distribute, or earn from it — which attracts liability under Section 15(1) or 15(2) but not the higher punishment of Section 15(3).
Accidental or unknowing retention of child pornographic material where there is no evidence of any commercial intent or awareness of the content.
Storage by law enforcement officials, forensic analysts, or child protection authorities in their official capacity during an investigation.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether conduct falls within 'commercial purpose' under Section 15(3) determines the severity of punishment: a first conviction triggers mandatory minimum imprisonment of three years extendable to five years (with fine), and a subsequent conviction carries a mandatory minimum of five years extendable to seven years with fine — significantly harsher than the penalties under Sections 15(1) and 15(2). The classification as commercial purpose elevates the offence to reflect the organised, exploitative, and profit-driven nature of child sexual abuse material trafficking.

definitions.law_name: Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012
definitions.definition: Conspiracy, as used under the Act, refers to an agreement or engagement between two or more persons for the doing of an offence under this Act, where an act or illegal omission takes place in pursuance of that agreement and in order to the doing of that offence. It forms the second limb of abetment under Section 16, and an act or offence is committed in consequence of such conspiracy when it is carried out in pursuance of the conspiratorial agreement.
definitions.plain_english: Conspiracy means when two or more people plan or agree together to commit a sexual offence against a child under this law, and then at least one actual step or wrongful act is taken to carry out that plan. It does not matter if the main offence is ultimately completed — the planning and the step taken together are enough. Any person who was part of the agreement can be held responsible even if they did not personally commit the final act.
real_world_examples: A school bus driver and a teacher in a Delhi school secretly agree to lure a minor student to an isolated room after school hours for the purpose of sexual assault; the driver acts as a lookout while the teacher commits the act — both are liable as conspirators under Section 16.

In Mumbai, a group of men operating a child trafficking network plan and coordinate the movement of a minor girl from Bihar to Maharashtra for sexual exploitation; their coordinated planning and execution constitutes conspiracy under the Act.

A relative and a family friend in Chennai agree over phone calls to arrange repeated access to a child in their care for the purpose of sexual abuse; the relative provides access while the friend commits the assault — both are conspirators.

Two individuals in Hyderabad conspire online to produce child pornographic material by assigning roles — one to coerce the child and another to record — and carry out the plan; their prior agreement and coordinated action constitute conspiracy under Section 16.

A hostel warden and an outsider in Kolkata agree that the outsider will be granted night-time access to a minor resident for sexual purposes in exchange for money; the warden opening the gate in furtherance of this agreement constitutes an act in pursuance of the conspiracy.
what_it_covers: An agreement between two or more persons to commit any sexual offence under POCSO, provided at least one act or illegal omission is carried out in furtherance of that agreement.

Situations where roles are divided among conspirators — such as one person arranging access to the child while another commits the assault — and all parties are aware of and assent to the common criminal purpose.
Remote or indirect participants who plan the offence but are not physically present at the scene of the crime, as long as they were party to the conspiracy and an act was done in pursuance of it.

Conspiracies formed prior to the commission of the offence, including planning through electronic communication, phone calls, or in-person meetings, where the agreed offence is subsequently attempted or committed.
what_it_excludes: A mere agreement to commit an offence where no act or illegal omission whatsoever takes place in pursuance of that conspiracy — the Act requires that an overt step must occur for conspiracy-based abetment to be established.
Unilateral planning or intention by a single person to commit an offence, since conspiracy by definition requires engagement with at least one other person.
Acts of facilitation that occur without any prior agreement or shared intent between the parties, which may instead fall under the 'aiding' limb of abetment rather than conspiracy.

Persons who are innocently or unknowingly involved without any knowledge of or consent to the criminal purpose, such as a transport worker who unknowingly carries a child being trafficked without awareness of the offence.
definitions.why_it_matters: A person found to be party to a conspiracy under Section 16 is treated as an abettor of the offence and, under Section 17, is punishable with the same punishment prescribed for the primary offence under the Act if the abetted act is committed in consequence of the abetment — meaning conspirators face identical penal consequences as the direct perpetrator. This definition is critical because it extends criminal liability beyond the actual offender to all who planned or coordinated the sexual offence against a child.

definitions.definition: A Court of Session, as used in the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012, refers to the principal criminal court of original jurisdiction in a district established under the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, which is designated by the State Government, in consultation with the Chief Justice of the High Court, to function as a Special Court for the speedy trial of offences under this Act. Where no Special Court has been designated, the Court of Session exercises the jurisdiction and receives reports under this Act directly.
definitions.plain_english: A Court of Session is the main criminal court at the district level in India, headed by a Sessions Judge. Under POCSO, the State Government picks one such court in each district and designates it as a 'Special Court' to handle child sexual abuse cases quickly. If no Special Court has been set up yet in a district, the regular Court of Session itself handles POCSO matters directly.
real_world_examples: In Pune district, the State Government notifies the Second Additional Sessions Court as the designated Special Court under POCSO; until that notification, the Principal Sessions Court in Pune directly receives police reports about child sexual assault cases.

A Special Juvenile Police Unit in Chennai, after registering a case of penetrative sexual assault on a minor, reports the matter within 24 hours to the designated Court of Session (Special Court) in the district, as required under Section 19(6) of the Act.

In a tribal district of Jharkhand where no Special Court has yet been designated, the local police report a POCSO offence directly to the existing Court of Session, which then tries the accused using all powers of a Special Court.

The Rajasthan government, in consultation with the Chief Justice of the Rajasthan High Court, issues a gazette notification designating the Fast Track Court of Session in Jaipur as the Special Court for POCSO cases in Jaipur district.

A Court of Session in Hyderabad that had already been notified as a children's court under the Commissions for Protection of Child Rights Act, 2005, is automatically deemed to be a Special Court under POCSO Section 28, without requiring a fresh designation.
what_it_covers: A Sessions Court designated by the State Government via Official Gazette notification as the Special Court for a specific district to try POCSO offences.

A Court of Session previously notified as a children's court under the Commissions for Protection of Child Rights Act, 2005, which is deemed to be a Special Court under POCSO without a separate designation.

The regular Court of Session in a district where no Special Court has yet been designated, which directly receives reports from police or the Special Juvenile Police Unit under Section 19(6) and exercises all POCSO jurisdiction.

A Court of Session functioning as a Special Court that also has jurisdiction to try ancillary offences under Section 67B of the Information Technology Act, 2000, relating to child sexual abuse material online.
what_it_excludes: Magistrate courts (Chief Judicial Magistrate or Executive Magistrate courts), which do not have the status or powers of a Court of Session and cannot be designated as Special Courts under POCSO.
High Courts and the Supreme Court of India, which are superior courts and operate outside the framework of district-level Court of Session designation under this Act.
Family Courts or civil courts, which lack criminal jurisdiction and cannot be designated as a Court of Session for POCSO trial purposes.

A court designated under a special law for an entirely different subject matter (e.g., a Special Court for economic offences under PMLA) that has not been specifically notified for POCSO or children's rights purposes.
definitions.why_it_matters: The designation of a Court of Session as a Special Court directly determines which court has exclusive jurisdiction to try POCSO offences, ensuring speedy trial and child-friendly procedures; failure to have a designated Special Court means all reporting obligations under Section 19(6) and trial powers default to the ordinary Court of Session, which must then exercise the full powers of a Special Court including those protective procedures mandated for child victims.

definitions.definition: "Culpable mental state" includes intention, motive, knowledge of a fact and the belief in, or reason to believe, a fact, as used in the context of prosecutions under the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012, where the Special Court shall presume its existence on the part of the accused, and it shall be a defence for the accused to prove beyond reasonable doubt that he had no such mental state.
definitions.plain_english: Culpable mental state refers to the guilty mind or mental awareness behind committing an act — it includes having an intention to do something, a motive for doing it, knowing that a fact exists, or having reason to believe something is true. Under POCSO, the law automatically assumes that an accused person had this guilty mindset when charged with an offence. The burden then falls on the accused to prove, beyond reasonable doubt, that they did not have such a mental state at the time of the act.
real_world_examples: A 35-year-old man in Mumbai repeatedly visits a 13-year-old girl's school under the pretext of being a distant relative and engages in unwanted physical contact — the court presumes he acted with intention and sexual intent, and he must prove he had no culpable mental state.

An operator of a cyber café in Delhi allows a minor to view and download sexually explicit material involving children; the court presumes the operator had knowledge of what the child was accessing, and the operator must rebut this presumption beyond reasonable doubt.

A teacher in a Bengaluru school repeatedly calls a 10-year-old student to a private room and touches the child inappropriately; the court presumes the teacher acted with motive and intention, placing the burden on the teacher to disprove the culpable mental state.

A stepfather in Kolkata claims he accidentally touched his 8-year-old stepdaughter while helping her bathe; the Special Court presumes he had knowledge or reason to believe his actions constituted sexual assault, and he must prove absence of culpable mental state beyond reasonable doubt.

A distributor of pornographic material in Chennai is found to have circulated videos involving children, claiming he was unaware of the content; the court presumes he had reason to believe the material was child pornography, and he must rebut this presumption to escape liability.
what_it_covers: Intention: where the accused deliberately planned or chose to commit the act against the child.
Motive: an underlying purpose or reason driving the accused to commit the offence, such as gratification or coercion.
Knowledge of a fact: where the accused was aware of a relevant fact, such as knowing the victim was a child or that the material was pornographic in nature.

Belief in or reason to believe a fact: where the accused had sufficient grounds to believe a particular fact existed, even if not certain, such as having reason to believe the person being photographed was a minor.
The legal presumption triggered in all POCSO prosecutions requiring proof of mental state, shifting the evidential burden to the accused.
what_it_excludes: Purely accidental acts where there is no element of intention, motive, knowledge or reason to believe — though the accused must prove this beyond reasonable doubt before the Special Court.
Negligence or carelessness alone, which does not amount to culpable mental state as defined under this section, since the definition requires intention, motive, knowledge, or reason to believe.

Acts committed under genuine, provable ignorance of a fact, where the accused can demonstrate beyond reasonable doubt that they had no knowledge, motive, intention or reason to believe the relevant fact existed.
Civil or administrative liability determinations, as culpable mental state under Section 30 applies exclusively to criminal prosecutions before the Special Court under POCSO.
definitions.why_it_matters: The presumption of culpable mental state under Section 30 significantly shifts the burden of proof onto the accused in POCSO prosecutions — once the prosecution establishes the act, the Special Court presumes the existence of the required guilty mind, and failure by the accused to rebut this presumption beyond reasonable doubt results in conviction. This directly governs the outcome of offences such as penetrative sexual assault, sexual assault, sexual harassment, use of a child for pornographic purposes, and other POCSO offences that require proof of a mental element.

definitions.definition: The 'designated authority' means such authority as may be prescribed by the Central Government under Section 45, to whom any person who stores or possesses pornographic material in any form involving a child is required to delete, destroy, or report such material under sub-section (1) of Section 15 of this Act.
definitions.plain_english: The 'designated authority' is a government-appointed body or official that a person must contact and report to if they come across or accidentally possess child pornographic material. Instead of keeping or sharing such material, the person is legally required to report it to this authority. definitions.law_name: Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012
definitions.definition: The term 'digital' is not formally defined in the Act but is used in Section 11 to describe a mode or medium through which sexual harassment of a child may be perpetrated, including digital means of repeatedly following, watching, or contacting a child, and digital modes of threatening to depict a child's body or sexual involvement. It encompasses all forms of digitally encoded communication, content, or contact transmitted via electronic devices, networks, or platforms.
definitions.plain_english: In this law, 'digital' refers to any method of communication or content creation that uses digital technology — such as smartphones, computers, tablets, the internet, or apps — to contact, follow, watch, or threaten a child. This includes sending messages, making video calls, sharing images, or using social media platforms. It covers any action carried out through a device or network that converts information into digital signals.
real_world_examples: An adult repeatedly sends WhatsApp messages or voice notes to a child with sexual intent, constituting digital contact under Section 11(iv) of the Act.
A perpetrator threatens to upload a morphed or real video of a child in a sexual act on YouTube or Instagram unless the child complies with demands, amounting to digital threat under Section 11(v).

An offender uses a gaming platform or online chat application such as Discord to continuously monitor, follow, and contact a minor for pornographic purposes, qualifying as digital means of sexual harassment.
A person sends sexually explicit images or videos to a child via email or Telegram, using digital media to expose the child to pornographic content under Section 11(iii) read with Section 11(iv).

An accused uses a deepfake application to create a digitally manipulated video depicting a child in a sexual act and threatens to circulate it on social media, triggering Section 11(v) through digital mode.
what_it_covers: Sending sexually explicit messages, images, or videos to a child via smartphones, computers, or tablets through apps like WhatsApp, Telegram, or email.
Using social media platforms, online gaming environments, or chat applications to repeatedly follow, watch, or contact a child with sexual intent.
Creating or using digitally generated, morphed, or manipulated images and videos depicting a child in a sexual act and threatening to circulate them online.
Contacting a child through digital platforms such as Instagram, Snapchat, or dating apps for pornographic purposes or enticing them with gratification.
Using digital recording devices or screen-capture tools to covertly record a child and subsequently threatening the child with the footage.
what_it_excludes: Physical, in-person contact or gestures made directly to a child without any involvement of a digital device or network, which fall under other clauses of Section 11.
Purely analogue or non-digital media such as printed photographs, handwritten letters, or traditional film-based depictions that are not encoded in digital format.
Broadcast through purely analogue television or radio signals that do not involve digital encoding or transmission technology.
Actions carried out solely through conventional voice telephone calls over analogue landlines with no digital component.
Non-technological means of following or watching a child, such as physically trailing a child in a public place without the use of any digital device.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act qualifies as carried out through 'digital' means determines whether it constitutes sexual harassment under Section 11(iv) or Section 11(v) of the POCSO Act, which is a cognisable and non-bailable offence attracting imprisonment of up to three years under Section 12. Establishing the digital nature of the contact or threat is also critical for invoking the Information Technology Act, 2000 concurrently and for preserving digital evidence during investigation.

definitions.law_name: Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012
definitions.definition: 'Domestic relationship' shall have the same meaning as assigned to it in clause (f) of section 2 of the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 (43 of 2005), which defines it as a relationship between two persons who live or have, at any point of time, lived together in a shared household, when they are related by consanguinity, marriage, or through a relationship in the nature of marriage, adoption or are family members living together as a joint family.
definitions.plain_english: A 'domestic relationship' refers to any close personal or family bond where two people live, or have lived together, in the same home. This includes relationships by blood, marriage, adoption, or even live-in arrangements that resemble marriage. Under POCSO, this term is used to identify when an accused person had such a close household connection to the child's parent or guardian, which makes the offence more serious.
real_world_examples: A stepfather who lives in the same house as the child's mother and the child — since he is in a domestic relationship with the child's mother, any sexual offence he commits against the child would be treated as aggravated under POCSO.

A live-in partner of the child's mother who shares the household with the family and commits penetrative sexual assault on the child — this qualifies as aggravated penetrative sexual assault because of the domestic relationship with the parent.

A maternal uncle who permanently resides in the same shared household as a joint family member and sexually assaults the child — the domestic relationship by consanguinity and cohabitation brings the offence within the aggravated category.

A man who was previously in a live-in relationship with the child's mother and lived in the same household, even if he has since moved out, may still be covered since the definition includes those who 'have lived' together in a domestic relationship.

A man married to the child's mother through a customary marriage recognised under personal law, living in the same home, who commits sexual assault on the child — the marital domestic relationship with the parent elevates the offence to aggravated sexual assault under Section 9 of POCSO.
what_it_covers: A live-in partner or spouse of the child's parent who resides in the shared household with the child.
A relative related by blood or adoption who lives or has lived in the same household as a joint family member.
A person in a relationship in the nature of marriage with the child's parent, sharing the same household, even without formal legal marriage.
Former cohabitants who previously lived in a domestic relationship in the shared household, even if they no longer reside there at the time of the offence.
Members of a joint family residing together, connected by consanguinity or adoption, who share the household with the child.
what_it_excludes: A stranger or acquaintance who has no cohabitation history or family connection with the child or the child's parent.
A neighbour, teacher, or family friend who visits the household regularly but has never lived there in any familial or quasi-familial capacity.
A distant relative living in a separate household with no shared residence history, even if they are related by blood.
A landlord or paying guest who occupies a separate unit in the same building but does not share the household as a family unit.
Professional caregivers such as domestic workers or babysitters who work in the home but do not reside there as part of a domestic relationship.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an accused person had a 'domestic relationship' with the child's parent or guardian directly determines if the offence is classified as 'aggravated penetrative sexual assault' under Section 5 or 'aggravated sexual assault' under Section 9 of POCSO, which carry significantly higher mandatory minimum punishments than basic offences. This classification also affects bail conditions, sentencing, and the nature of the Special Court proceedings.

definitions.definition: The term 'electronic' is not formally defined in the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012, but is used to denote any mode of communication, contact, transmission, or depiction carried out through electronic signals, networks, or devices, including but not limited to mobile phones, internet platforms, email, messaging applications, and electronic media, as distinct from purely physical or print-based means.
definitions.plain_english: Electronic refers to anything done using electronic devices or networks — such as mobile phones, the internet, computers, or apps — to communicate, contact, transmit, or display content. In this law, it describes one of the ways a person can sexually harass or exploit a child without being physically present. For example, sending threatening or inappropriate messages to a child over WhatsApp or contacting a child repeatedly through social media would count as 'electronic' means.
real_world_examples: An adult in Mumbai repeatedly sends sexually suggestive text messages and WhatsApp voice notes to a 14-year-old, constituting contact 'through electronic means' under Section 11 of POCSO.

A perpetrator in Delhi uses Instagram direct messages to constantly follow and contact a 12-year-old child, watch her stories, and send her unsolicited content — amounting to electronic surveillance and contact under Section 11.

A person in Chennai threatens to upload a morphed or real intimate image of a minor on YouTube unless the child complies with demands — this use of electronic media for threats falls under Section 11(v) of POCSO.
An accused in Bengaluru sends pornographic video links to a child through email repeatedly, using electronic means to contact the child for pornographic purposes under Section 11.
A teacher in Kolkata uses a school WhatsApp group to share obscene content or make gestures visible to a child via a video call, constituting electronic contact with sexual intent under Section 11.

A man in Hyderabad livestreams a minor's exploitation on a private internet channel — classified as use of electronic form under Section 13 read alongside the electronic-means framework of Section 11.
semantic_tags: electronic means of following or watching
what_it_covers: Contact made through mobile phones, SMS, WhatsApp, Telegram, or other messaging applications directed at a child with sexual intent.
Repeatedly following, watching, or monitoring a child through social media platforms, email, or any internet-based service using electronic networks.
Threats made via electronic channels — such as email, messaging apps, or video platforms — to use real or fabricated depictions of a child's body in a sexual context.
Use of internet or electronic broadcasting to transmit, publish, or distribute pornographic material involving a child as described in Section 13.
Recording a child's statement by audio-video electronic means as referenced in Section 26, ensuring procedural compliance in investigations.
what_it_excludes: Purely physical or in-person acts of sexual harassment or contact that involve no electronic device or network, such as direct verbal utterances or physical gestures.
Print-based material — such as newspapers, books, or physical photographs — which fall under 'printed form' rather than 'electronic form' as used in Section 13.
Traditional postal or written correspondence that does not travel through any electronic signal or network medium.
Purely mechanical or analogue devices that do not use electronic signals or digital transmission to communicate or display content.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether conduct qualifies as occurring through 'electronic means' determines if an offence of sexual harassment under Section 11 or use of a child for pornographic purposes under Section 13 is established even without physical proximity between the accused and the child. Establishing the electronic nature of contact or transmission is critical to prosecuting cyber-enabled POCSO offences and to invoking the evidentiary and procedural provisions under the Act.
