definitions.law_name: Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012
definitions.definition: A false complaint is a complaint made against any person in respect of an offence under sections 3, 5, 7, or 9 of this Act, which is knowingly untrue and made solely with the intention to humiliate, extort, threaten, or defame the accused person. Where such a false complaint is made by a person who is not a child against a child, knowing it to be false, it constitutes an aggravated form that victimizes the child.
definitions.plain_english: A false complaint means when someone knowingly lies about another person committing a child sexual abuse offence under this law, and their only reason for doing so is to harm that person's reputation, force money from them, or intimidate them. It is treated as a serious wrong under this law. However, if the person making the false complaint is a child, they cannot be punished for it.
real_world_examples: A divorced mother in Delhi files a complaint under Section 3 (penetrative sexual assault) against her ex-husband, falsely alleging he assaulted their child, with the sole motive of gaining custody and extracting a higher alimony settlement.
A business rival in Mumbai coaches a child to file a false sexual harassment complaint under Section 9 against a competing shopkeeper to destroy his business reputation and drive away customers.

A landlord in Chennai falsely accuses a tenant's adult son of sexually assaulting a neighbour's child under Section 7 (sexual assault) to coerce the tenant into vacating the premises without paying pending dues.

An adult in Kolkata, in a personal vendetta, files a police complaint falsely implicating a schoolteacher under Section 5 (aggravated penetrative sexual assault), knowing the allegation is untrue, intending to get the teacher dismissed and publicly shamed.

A neighbour in Jaipur, angry over a property dispute, provides false information to the police claiming they witnessed a man commit an offence under Section 9 against a child living next door, with the intent to threaten and defame the man.

A woman in Hyderabad threatens her estranged brother-in-law with filing a POCSO complaint against him unless he signs over his share of ancestral property, and subsequently files one when he refuses, purely for extortion.
semantic_tags: victimization of child by false allegation
what_it_covers: A complaint filed by an adult against another adult alleging a POCSO offence under sections 3, 5, 7, or 9, which is knowingly untrue and made solely to humiliate or defame the accused.
False information provided to a police officer or authority about an offence under sections 3, 5, 7, or 9, with the sole intent to extort money or threaten the implicated person.
A complaint filed by a non-child person falsely implicating a child as a victim or perpetrator under this Act, knowing it to be false, thereby victimizing that child.
Any statement or allegation made with the sole motive to defame a person, even if dressed as a genuine complaint, as long as it pertains to offences under the specified sections.
what_it_excludes: A complaint made in good faith by a person who genuinely but mistakenly believed the offence occurred — the element of knowing falsity and sole malicious intent must be established.
A false complaint made by a child — the Act expressly states no punishment shall be imposed on a child who makes a false complaint or provides false information.

Complaints relating to offences under sections of this Act other than sections 3, 5, 7, and 9 (for example, a false complaint about child pornography under Section 13 does not fall within the scope of Section 22 punishment).
Cases where a person makes an erroneous complaint arising from misunderstanding or coercion by a third party, as the intent to humiliate, extort, or defame must be the sole driving motive.
definitions.why_it_matters: If a complaint is found to be a false complaint under Section 22, the person who made it can be imprisoned for up to six months and/or fined, or up to one year if filed against a child; this provision acts as a critical safeguard against misuse of the POCSO Act while also protecting genuine victims from having their complaints dismissed as false without clear proof of malicious intent.

definitions.law_name: Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012
definitions.definition: False information, as used under Section 22 of the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012, refers to any information provided by a person against another person in respect of an offence under sections 3, 5, 7, or 9 of the Act, which is knowingly untrue and is provided solely with the intention to humiliate, extort, threaten, or defame that person. Where such false information is provided by a person other than a child against a child, knowing it to be false, thereby victimising the child, it constitutes a graver form of the offence under the same section.
definitions.plain_english: False information means deliberately giving wrong or made-up information to authorities about someone supposedly committing a child sexual offence, when the person providing it knows the information is untrue. The key requirement is that the person giving this false information must be doing so on purpose — to harm, embarrass, blackmail, or damage the reputation of the accused. If a child provides false information, they cannot be punished for it. However, an adult who knowingly gives false information against a child to get the child into trouble faces stricter punishment.
real_world_examples: A neighbour in a Delhi housing society, locked in a property dispute with another resident, falsely reports to the police that the resident has sexually assaulted a minor child in the building, knowing fully well no such incident occurred, intending to get the person arrested and humiliated.

A woman in a matrimonial dispute in Mumbai provides a written statement to the Child Welfare Committee falsely alleging that her estranged husband's brother committed penetrative sexual assault on their young child, solely to gain leverage in custody proceedings and extort a financial settlement.

A disgruntled domestic worker in Chennai, after being dismissed from service, approaches the Special Juvenile Police Unit and provides a fabricated account claiming her former employer sexually harassed a minor domestic worker at the household, with the intention of defaming the employer.

A rival shopkeeper in a small town in Uttar Pradesh, seeking to destroy the reputation of a competitor, approaches the local police station and provides false information that the competitor committed aggravated sexual assault on a child, with no factual basis, purely to threaten and financially ruin the competitor.

An adult family member in a Kolkata household, during a bitter inheritance dispute, files a false complaint at a police station and simultaneously provides false supporting information alleging that another family member sexually assaulted a minor grandchild, knowing the allegation is entirely fabricated.
what_it_covers: A written or oral statement given to police or any authority about an offence under sections 3, 5, 7, or 9 of POCSO, which the person providing it knows to be factually untrue.
Information provided with the sole and deliberate intention to humiliate, extort money or benefit from, threaten, or damage the reputation of the person falsely accused.

False information provided by an adult person (not a child) against a child, with the knowledge that the information is false, thereby causing the child to be treated as a suspect or offender under the Act.

Any supporting documentation, statements, or material submitted to authorities as part of a false report regarding penetrative sexual assault, aggravated penetrative sexual assault, sexual assault, or aggravated sexual assault under the enumerated sections.
what_it_excludes: Information provided in good faith that later turns out to be incorrect or mistaken, where there was no deliberate intent to deceive or harm — an honest but erroneous complaint does not qualify as false information.
False information provided by a child, who is fully exempt from any punishment under Section 22 regardless of the falsity of the information given.

False information relating to offences under sections of POCSO other than sections 3, 5, 7, and 9 — Section 22 is specifically limited to complaints or information concerning those four enumerated offence sections.

Situations where the false information was provided due to coercion, duress, or manipulation by a third party, which may negate the element of sole intention to humiliate, extort, threaten, or defame.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a statement constitutes 'false information' under Section 22 directly determines criminal liability: a person proven to have provided false information solely to humiliate, extort, threaten, or defame faces imprisonment up to six months and/or fine, while an adult who knowingly provides false information against a child faces imprisonment up to one year and/or fine. This definition also serves as a critical safeguard to prevent misuse of POCSO while balancing protection of genuine complainants and child victims.

definitions.law_name: Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012
definitions.definition: When a child is subjected to sexual assault by one or more persons of a group in furtherance of their common intention, each of such persons shall be deemed to have committed gang sexual assault within the meaning of clause (g) of Section 9, and each of such persons shall be liable for that act in the same manner as if it were done by him alone.
definitions.plain_english: Gang sexual assault occurs when two or more people act together with a shared plan or intention to sexually assault a child. Every person who is part of the group is treated as equally guilty, even if not every member directly committed the act. This means the law holds each participant responsible as though they personally carried out the assault.
real_world_examples: A group of men in a village in Uttar Pradesh collectively assault a minor girl after forcibly taking her to an isolated field; all members of the group are charged with gang sexual assault under Section 9 even though only two physically committed the act.

A gang of teenage boys in a Mumbai slum area, acting on a pre-agreed plan, sexually assault a younger child from their neighbourhood; each boy is held liable under Section 9(g) for gang sexual assault regardless of their individual role.

A child labourer in a factory in Tamil Nadu is sexually assaulted by the factory owner and two supervisors acting together; all three are prosecuted for gang sexual assault as they shared a common intention to commit the act.

A group of men in Delhi lure a minor girl under the pretext of offering work and then sexually assault her collectively; each person present and participating in the common intention is charged with gang sexual assault under POCSO Section 9.

During a communal disturbance in a city in Rajasthan, multiple individuals from a mob sexually assault a child victim; all participants sharing the common intention are deemed to have committed gang sexual assault and face aggravated charges.
what_it_covers: Two or more persons who jointly assault a child with a shared common intention, even if only one physically commits the sexual act.
Each individual member of the group, including those who may have only facilitated, restrained the child, or stood guard while others committed the act, provided they shared the common intention.
Situations where a child is assaulted sequentially by members of the same group acting pursuant to the same plan or common intention, not necessarily simultaneously.
Cases where the group is informal or ad hoc, meaning there is no requirement of a pre-existing organised gang — a spontaneously formed group with a common intention suffices.

Each accused being held individually liable for the full offence as if they had committed the assault alone, attracting the enhanced punishment prescribed for aggravated sexual assault under Section 10.
what_it_excludes: A single individual acting alone who commits sexual assault on a child — this falls under sexual assault or aggravated sexual assault on other grounds, not gang sexual assault.
Persons who had no knowledge of and did not share the common intention of the group to commit sexual assault on the child, even if they were physically present at the scene.
Situations where two or more persons independently and separately commit sexual assault on the same child at different times without any shared plan or common intention linking their acts.
Mere association or membership in a group that committed an offence, absent proof of sharing the common intention to commit gang sexual assault on the child.
Abetors or conspirators who are prosecuted under separate provisions for abetment or conspiracy, and whose liability is governed under those distinct heads rather than the gang sexual assault clause.
definitions.why_it_matters: Classification as gang sexual assault under Section 9(g) elevates the offence from sexual assault to aggravated sexual assault, thereby triggering the enhanced punishment under Section 10 of POCSO, which prescribes imprisonment of not less than five years extendable to seven years along with a fine. This classification also ensures that each member of the group bears full individual criminal liability for the entirety of the act, preventing any accused from escaping punishment by arguing a limited or indirect role.

definitions.law_name: Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012
definitions.definition: The term 'gratification' is not formally defined in the Act but is used in Section 11 to denote any benefit, reward, consideration, or inducement — whether monetary, material, or non-material — given to a child to entice or persuade the child to participate in pornographic purposes. It encompasses any form of advantage offered to a child as an incentive in the context of sexual exploitation.
definitions.plain_english: Gratification means any kind of reward, gift, money, favour, or benefit given to a child to lure or persuade them into participating in pornographic activities. It does not have to be cash — it can be anything of value like food, toys, mobile phones, affection, or promises. The key idea is that something is offered to the child to get them to cooperate with a person who has sexual or exploitative intent.
real_world_examples: An adult in Mumbai offers a 12-year-old child chocolates and a new mobile phone to pose for obscene photographs intended for online distribution — the chocolates and phone constitute gratification under Section 11.

A person in Delhi promises to pay a poor child from a slum a sum of money every week in exchange for the child appearing in pornographic video content recorded on a smartphone — the promised money is gratification.

In a small town in Uttar Pradesh, a shopkeeper gives a child free snacks and soft drinks regularly to entice the child to exhibit their body for the shopkeeper's voyeuristic purposes — the free snacks constitute gratification.

An agent in Chennai promises a teenage child from a financially distressed family admission to a reputed school and payment of school fees in exchange for participation in the production of child pornographic material — the admission and fees are gratification.

A person in Kolkata offers a child gifts such as clothes, toys, and pocket money over several weeks to build trust and eventually persuade the child to participate in the creation of obscene content for pornographic purposes — all such gifts amount to gratification.
what_it_covers: Cash payments or promises of money given to a child to participate in pornographic activities.
Non-monetary rewards such as gifts, food, toys, gadgets, or clothing offered to a child to entice participation in pornographic purposes.
Intangible benefits such as promises of education, employment, protection, or special favours given to a child to secure their cooperation in sexual exploitation.
Repeated small favours or incremental benefits given to a child as part of a grooming process intended to eventually lead to pornographic exploitation.
Any consideration — direct or indirect — offered to a third party (such as a parent or guardian) on behalf of the child to facilitate the child's participation in pornographic content.
what_it_excludes: Legitimate gifts or rewards given to a child in a normal familial, educational, or social context that have no connection to sexual intent or pornographic purposes.
Compensation or payments made to child artists engaged in lawful, non-pornographic media productions that do not involve sexual exploitation.
Threats, coercion, or force used against a child — these do not constitute gratification, which requires a positive inducement rather than compulsion.
Psychological manipulation or emotional grooming that does not involve any tangible or intangible benefit or reward being offered to the child.
Benefits provided to a child under statutory welfare schemes or court-ordered support unconnected to any sexual or pornographic intent.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act constitutes 'gratification' under Section 11 is critical to establishing the offence of sexual harassment of a child, specifically the limb that penalises enticing a child for pornographic purposes — a conviction can result in imprisonment of up to three years under Section 12. Proof of gratification helps establish the accused's sexual intent and the deliberate, calculated nature of the exploitation, which can also support related charges under Sections 13 and 14 concerning use of a child for pornographic purposes.

definitions.law_name: Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012
definitions.definition: The term 'grievous hurt' is not separately defined in the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012, and accordingly carries the meaning assigned to it under Section 320 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860, which enumerates eight specific categories of hurt designated as grievous, including emasculation, permanent privation of sight or hearing, permanent disfiguration of the head or face, fracture or dislocation of a bone or tooth, and any hurt which endangers life or causes the sufferer to be in severe bodily pain or unable to follow ordinary pursuits for twenty days. In the context of POCSO, 'grievous hurt' refers to such serious physical injury caused to a child as a direct consequence of penetrative sexual assault or sexual assault.
definitions.plain_english: Grievous hurt means very serious physical injury — not just minor pain or bruising, but harm that is severe enough to permanently damage a part of the body, break bones, endanger life, or leave the child unable to carry on normal daily activities for at least twenty days. It is a legally recognised category of serious bodily harm borrowed from the Indian Penal Code. When a sexual assault on a child causes this level of injury, the crime becomes much more serious under POCSO.
real_world_examples: A child victim of penetrative sexual assault in Mumbai sustains a fractured pelvis requiring hospitalisation and surgery for over a month, rendering the child unable to walk or attend school — this constitutes grievous hurt elevating the offence to aggravated penetrative sexual assault under Section 5 of POCSO.

A six-year-old girl in Delhi is sexually assaulted and suffers permanent damage to her internal reproductive organs, causing lasting physical impairment — the permanent injury to internal organs qualifies as grievous hurt under IPC Section 320 and aggravates the POCSO offence.

A young boy in Chennai is assaulted and sustains burns to his genital area from a heated object used during the assault, causing severe pain and hospitalisation for more than three weeks — the combination of grievous hurt and use of a heated substance triggers Section 5 aggravated penetrative sexual assault.

A twelve-year-old child in Kolkata suffers a dislocated hip joint and torn tissue during a sexual assault by a neighbour, leaving the child bedridden and unable to perform ordinary activities for over a month — this dislocation of a bone constitutes grievous hurt under IPC Section 320 read with POCSO Section 5.

A child in a remand home in Hyderabad is sexually assaulted by a staff member and loses vision in one eye due to physical force applied during the assault — permanent privation of sight is expressly listed as grievous hurt, and the dual aggravating factors of staff status and grievous hurt apply under Section 5.

A ten-year-old tribal girl in Jharkhand is gang-assaulted and sustains multiple bone fractures and life-threatening internal bleeding — the grievous hurt caused alongside gang assault makes the case punishable under the most severe provisions of POCSO Sections 5 and 6.
what_it_covers: Permanent loss or impairment of a bodily organ or faculty of the child caused during sexual assault, such as loss of vision, hearing, or damage to reproductive organs.
Fracture or dislocation of any bone or tooth of the child resulting from the force used during penetrative sexual assault or sexual assault.
Any injury to the child that endangers life, causes severe bodily pain, or renders the child unable to perform ordinary activities for a period of twenty days or more.
Permanent disfigurement of the head or face of the child caused in the course of committing sexual assault.
Destruction or permanent impairing of the powers of any member or joint of the child's body as a direct result of the assault.
what_it_excludes: Minor bruising, superficial cuts, or temporary soreness that heals within a few days without medical intervention — such injuries constitute ordinary 'hurt' under IPC, not grievous hurt.
Psychological or mental trauma alone, however severe, does not constitute grievous hurt, which requires demonstrable physical bodily injury of a specified serious nature.
Temporary discomfort or pain lasting fewer than twenty days and not involving any fracture, permanent damage, or life-threatening condition falls outside the definition.
Injuries that are self-inflicted by the child or caused by a third party unconnected to the sexual assault are not covered as grievous hurt within the POCSO context.
Non-physical harms such as financial loss, reputational harm, or emotional distress caused to the child's family are entirely outside the scope of this term.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an assault causes 'grievous hurt' is a critical aggravating factor under POCSO: if penetrative sexual assault causes grievous hurt, the offence is classified as aggravated penetrative sexual assault under Section 5(l), attracting the enhanced punishment prescribed in Section 6, which provides for rigorous imprisonment of not less than twenty years extendable to imprisonment for life or death. Similarly, Section 9 elevates sexual assault to aggravated sexual assault when grievous hurt is caused, triggering the higher punishment under Section 10.

definitions.definition: A 'guardian' in relation to a child means any person who has been entrusted with the care and custody of the child by a court of law or any other authority, or who has otherwise assumed responsibility for the care, welfare, and protection of the child, whether through blood, adoption, marriage, foster care, or any other domestic arrangement. The term includes persons standing in loco parentis to the child.
definitions.plain_english: A guardian is any adult who is legally or practically responsible for the care and protection of a child. This could be someone appointed by a court, a foster parent, a relative who has taken in the child, or any other person who has taken on the role of looking after the child in place of the parents. The key idea is that this person holds a position of trust and responsibility over the child.
real_world_examples: A maternal uncle in Mumbai who has taken custody of his orphaned niece following the death of her parents and is responsible for her daily care, education, and welfare acts as her guardian under POCSO.
A court in Delhi appoints a grandparent as the legal guardian of a child after both parents are found unfit due to substance abuse, making that grandparent accountable as a guardian under the Act.

A foster family in Chennai officially registered under the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015 and entrusted with a child by the Child Welfare Committee qualifies as guardians for the purpose of POCSO proceedings.

An elder sibling in Kolkata who has been formally entrusted by a court with the care of younger siblings following parental death assumes the role of guardian and has corresponding obligations and potential liability under POCSO.

An NGO-run children's home in Pune where staff members have been granted formal custodial responsibility by a Child Welfare Committee — those staff members in positions of direct care may be treated as persons standing in the guardian's role for purposes of Sections 40 and 41.
A stepparent in Hyderabad who has legally adopted the child after marrying the biological parent and now exercises full parental authority and responsibility qualifies as a guardian under the Act.
what_it_covers: A person appointed by a competent court as the legal guardian of a child, with formal custody and responsibility for the child's welfare.
A foster parent or foster family registered under applicable law and entrusted with the care of a child by a Child Welfare Committee or other authority.
A relative such as a grandparent, uncle, aunt, or elder sibling who has assumed de facto or de jure responsibility for the care and upbringing of the child in the absence of biological parents.
A stepparent who has legally adopted the child or otherwise assumed full custodial and parental responsibility through marriage to the biological parent.
An institution or its designated representative formally entrusted by a court or authority with the care and protection of a specific child.
what_it_excludes: A mere neighbor, family friend, or acquaintance who provides occasional informal assistance to a child but has not been entrusted with formal or substantive custodial responsibility.
A schoolteacher or tutor who exercises authority over a child only during school hours or in an educational context, without any broader custodial or welfare responsibility.
A biological parent who retains full parental rights and responsibilities, as they are governed by the concept of parenthood rather than guardianship under the Act.
A person who has only financial or property-related guardianship over a child's estate but exercises no role in the physical care, welfare, or day-to-day protection of the child.
Government officials such as police officers or social workers who come into contact with the child in a professional capacity but do not hold formal custodial responsibility.

definitions.definition: An 'illegal omission' under Section 16 refers to a failure to act where there exists a legal duty to act, which failure is intentionally used to aid or facilitate the commission of an offence under this Act, or takes place in pursuance of a conspiracy for the doing of such offence. It encompasses any deliberate refraining from action that, by its omission, enables, assists, or advances the commission of a sexual offence against a child.
definitions.plain_english: An illegal omission means deliberately doing nothing when you were legally required to act, and that deliberate inaction helps someone commit a crime against a child. For example, if a person who has a duty to protect or report stays silent or looks the other way so that an offence can take place, that silence or inaction is an 'illegal omission.' It is treated as seriously as actively helping someone commit the crime.
real_world_examples: A school principal in Mumbai becomes aware that a teacher is sexually assaulting a student but deliberately chooses not to report it to the police or Child Welfare Committee, thereby allowing the abuse to continue — this deliberate non-reporting constitutes an illegal omission under Section 16.

A hostel warden in Delhi knows that a senior student is regularly subjecting a junior child to sexual assault at night but intentionally fails to intervene or alert authorities, facilitating the ongoing offence through his omission.

A parent in Chennai is aware that their live-in domestic partner is sexually abusing their minor child but deliberately refrains from lodging a complaint or removing the child from harm's way, aiding the commission of the offence by doing nothing.

A doctor conducting a medical examination of a child in a Kolkata hospital discovers signs of sexual abuse but, having been bribed, intentionally omits to record the findings in the medical report or report it to the police, thereby facilitating concealment of the offence.

A child care institution supervisor in Hyderabad, aware of a conspiracy among staff members to exploit children residing in the shelter, deliberately fails to take any preventive action or make any disclosure, making his omission part of the conspiracy to commit the offence.
what_it_covers: A person with a legal duty to report child sexual abuse who intentionally stays silent to allow the offence to proceed or continue.
A conspirator's deliberate failure to perform an act required under an agreed plan, where that failure advances the commission of a sexual offence against a child.
A school, hospital, or institutional authority that intentionally refrains from taking protective or reporting action despite knowledge of ongoing sexual abuse of a child under their care.
Any deliberate withholding of information or action by a person legally bound to disclose or act, which thereby aids the perpetration of an offence under the Act.
A guardian or caretaker who knowingly omits to intervene or seek help when they have the capacity and legal obligation to do so, enabling the offence to occur.
what_it_excludes: Genuine ignorance or lack of awareness of the offence being committed — an omission that is not intentional or wilful does not qualify as an illegal omission.
Failure to act due to physical incapacity, mental illness, or circumstances entirely beyond the person's control, where no legal duty could reasonably be discharged.
Omissions by persons who have no legal duty or special responsibility toward the child victim and who are not party to any conspiracy to commit the offence.
Mere negligence or carelessness in not detecting or preventing an offence, where there is no deliberate intent to facilitate the commission of the offence.
Omissions that occur after the offence has already been fully completed, which cannot logically aid or facilitate the commission of the act.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act qualifies as an 'illegal omission' determines whether a person who did not physically participate in the offence can still be held liable for abetment under Section 16 of POCSO, attracting the same punishment prescribed for the primary offence. It triggers criminal liability for institutional gatekeepers, guardians, and co-conspirators whose deliberate inaction enables child sexual abuse, and directly determines whether charges of abetment can be framed and prosecuted.

definitions.definition: A person is said to instigate the doing of an offence under this Act when they, by wilful misrepresentation or by wilful concealment of a material fact which they are bound to disclose, voluntarily cause or procure, or attempt to cause or procure a thing to be done. Instigation also arises when a person directly urges, encourages, or incites another person to commit an offence under this Act. An act or offence is said to be committed in consequence of instigation when it is committed as a result of such urging, misrepresentation, or concealment.
definitions.plain_english: Instigation means actively encouraging, urging, or pushing another person to commit a sexual offence against a child. It also includes situations where someone deliberately lies or hides important facts to get another person to commit such an offence. In simple terms, if you convince, trick, or pressure someone into committing a crime against a child, you have instigated that crime. Even an attempt to cause someone to commit the offence counts as instigation under this law.
real_world_examples: A school teacher in Mumbai repeatedly tells a fellow staff member that a particular child is 'willing' and 'available', knowing this to be false, thereby encouraging the staff member to sexually assault the child — this constitutes instigation by wilful misrepresentation.

An adult relative in Delhi deliberately conceals from a household worker that the child left alone at home is a minor, encouraging the worker to engage in sexual conduct with the child — this amounts to instigation by wilful concealment of a material fact.
A pimp in Kolkata verbally urges a customer to commit penetrative sexual assault on a trafficked child by assuring him there will be no legal consequences, thereby directly instigating the offence.

A person in Chennai sends repeated messages and persuasive communications to another individual, urging and inciting them to create child pornography involving a specific child, thereby instigating the commission of an offence under POCSO.

A relative in Hyderabad who, knowing a child is being groomed, actively encourages another adult by saying the child 'wants it' and arranges for them to be alone together, instigating penetrative sexual assault.

A parent in Lucknow who, for monetary gain, pressures and convinces another person to commit sexual assault on their own child by misrepresenting the child's age as above 18 years, constituting instigation through wilful misrepresentation.

Attempts to cause or procure an act even if the offence is ultimately not committed, provided the instigation itself was made.
Psychological pressure, persuasion, or encouragement communicated through any means — verbal, written, or electronic — that motivates another to commit the offence.
what_it_excludes: Mere passive presence at the scene of a crime without any act of encouragement, urging, or misrepresentation does not constitute instigation.
Providing physical assistance or material aid to the commission of an offence, which falls under the separate limb of 'aiding' rather than instigation.
Entering into a conspiracy with one or more persons for the doing of an offence, which is governed by the conspiracy limb of abetment and not instigation.
Inadvertent or accidental disclosure of false information without wilful intent to cause or procure the commission of an offence.
Actions taken after the offence has already been committed, such as helping the offender escape, which may constitute a separate offence but do not amount to instigation.

definitions.definition: The Legal Services Authority refers to the authority constituted under the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987, which is obligated under Section 40 of the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012 to provide a lawyer to the family or guardian of a child who is unable to afford legal counsel for any offence under this Act.
definitions.plain_english: The Legal Services Authority is a government-established body that provides free legal help to people who cannot afford to hire a lawyer. Under the POCSO Act, if a child's family or guardian does not have the money to pay for a lawyer, this authority must arrange a free lawyer for them. This ensures that every child victim has proper legal representation in court, regardless of the family's financial situation.
real_world_examples: A daily-wage labourer in rural Rajasthan whose daughter has been sexually assaulted cannot afford an advocate. The District Legal Services Authority (DLSA) in Jaipur steps in and assigns a free lawyer to the family to represent them in the Special Court hearing the POCSO case.

A migrant worker family in Mumbai whose minor son has been abused by a neighbour approaches the Maharashtra State Legal Services Authority. The authority provides a trained panel advocate to assist the family throughout the trial under POCSO.

A tribal guardian in Jharkhand, who is the sole caretaker of a sexually assaulted child, is illiterate and financially destitute. The Jharkhand State Legal Services Authority assigns a lawyer to counsel and represent the guardian in all proceedings before the Children's Court.

After a POCSO offence is registered by a Special Juvenile Police Unit in Chennai, the investigating officer informs the child's poor parents about their right to free legal aid. The Tamil Nadu State Legal Services Authority is contacted and a panel advocate is promptly appointed to assist the family.

A single mother in Delhi working as a domestic helper cannot afford legal representation after her daughter is subjected to sexual harassment by a school staff member. The Delhi State Legal Services Authority provides a lawyer who assists in filing the case and appearing before the Special Court under POCSO.
what_it_covers: District Legal Services Authorities (DLSAs) constituted under the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987, which operate at the district level to provide free legal aid to eligible persons in POCSO cases.
State Legal Services Authorities (SLSAs) at the state level, which supervise and coordinate legal aid services and can assign lawyers in POCSO matters when district-level resources are insufficient.
Situations where the family or guardian of a child victim under POCSO is unable to afford a legal counsel, triggering the authority's mandatory obligation to provide a lawyer at no cost.
Panel advocates empanelled by the Legal Services Authority who are assigned to represent child victims' families before Special Courts or Courts of Session in POCSO proceedings.
what_it_excludes: Private law firms or privately retained advocates hired by families who can afford legal fees — these are not covered or provided by the Legal Services Authority.

The Special Public Prosecutor appointed by the government to conduct prosecution on behalf of the State — this is a separate mechanism under POCSO and is not the same as the Legal Services Authority's function.

Accused persons or offenders who seek legal representation — the Legal Services Authority's obligation under Section 40 of POCSO is specifically towards the family or guardian of the child victim, not the alleged perpetrator.
Legal aid for civil disputes or non-criminal matters unrelated to offences under POCSO — the provision in Section 40 is limited to offences under this Act only.
definitions.why_it_matters: The applicability of the Legal Services Authority under Section 40 determines whether a child victim's family receives state-funded legal representation, directly affecting the family's ability to participate meaningfully in POCSO proceedings and protect the child's interests. If this provision is triggered, the authority is under a mandatory obligation to provide a lawyer, ensuring that financial incapacity does not obstruct access to justice for child victims of sexual offences.

definitions.definition: Media, as used in the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012, refers to any medium or platform used for the creation, production, publication, transmission, distribution, or exhibition of content, including but not limited to print, electronic, digital, internet, television, film, photography, and any other technological form, through which material involving or relating to a child may be communicated or disseminated. The term encompasses all personnel, studios, and facilities engaged in such activities, who bear mandatory reporting obligations under the Act.
definitions.plain_english: Media means any channel, platform, or technology used to create, share, or spread content — this includes newspapers, TV channels, websites, social media platforms, film studios, and photography studios. Under this law, anyone working in these fields who comes across sexually exploitative material involving a child must report it to the police. The term is used broadly to cover both the organisations themselves and the people who work in them.
real_world_examples: A photo studio in Mumbai discovers during processing that images submitted for printing contain obscene photographs of a minor — the studio staff are obligated under Section 20 to immediately report this to the local police or Special Juvenile Police Unit.

A journalist working for a Hindi news channel in Delhi stumbles upon a video clip submitted as news footage that contains child pornographic content — as media personnel, they must report it to the SJPU without delay.

An employee at a digital advertising agency in Bengaluru notices that an advertisement campaign being produced involves suggestive or indecent depiction of a child for commercial gain — the agency and its personnel are required to report the matter under Section 20.

A social media content moderation team member employed by an Indian internet company identifies a post containing sexually exploitative images of children — the company, as an electronic media entity, must report such material to law enforcement authorities.

A film production house in Chennai finds during post-production review that raw footage includes the indecent representation of a minor actor — the studio personnel are covered under the media obligation and must report this immediately.

A newspaper in Kolkata receives a reader-submitted photograph that depicts a child in an obscene or sexually suggestive manner — the editorial and photographic staff are duty-bound under Section 20 to report it to the Special Juvenile Police Unit.

Print media outlets including newspapers and magazines, and their staff, who encounter or publish material involving obscene or pornographic depiction of children
Digital and internet-based platforms, social media companies, and online content distributors operating in India
Film production houses, studios, and photographic facilities that create, process, or store visual content involving children
Advertising agencies and OTT platforms that produce or transmit content where sexually exploitative child imagery may appear
what_it_excludes: Private individuals who are not employed in or operating a media, studio, or photographic facility — they are governed by Section 19 reporting obligations rather than Section 20
Educational or academic institutions that use recorded or printed material purely for bona fide child safety training or research, without any element of exploitation or dissemination
Law enforcement agencies and judiciary personnel who handle such material strictly in their official investigative or judicial capacity under the Act
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an entity qualifies as 'media' under this Act determines whether it is subject to the mandatory reporting obligation under Section 20, making its personnel legally required to report sexually exploitative child material to the Special Juvenile Police Unit or local police upon encountering it. definitions.law_name: Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012
definitions.definition: Medical examination of a child in respect of whom any offence has been committed under this Act shall be conducted in accordance with section 164A of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, and where the victim is a girl child, such examination shall be conducted by a woman doctor in the presence of a parent or trusted person, or in their absence, a woman nominated by the head of the medical institution. Where such medical examination is undertaken with the consent of the child's parents or guardian for purposes of medical examination or treatment, the provisions of sections 3 to 13 of the Act shall not apply.
definitions.plain_english: A medical examination under POCSO is a formal physical check-up of a child who may have been sexually abused, conducted by a doctor following specific legal rules to collect evidence and assess the child's health. If the child is a girl, only a woman doctor may conduct the exam, and a parent or trusted adult must usually be present. This examination can happen even before a police complaint is formally registered. When a doctor conducts a routine medical exam or treatment with the parents' consent, it is not treated as a sexual offence even if it involves physical contact.
real_world_examples: A 10-year-old girl in Mumbai is brought to a government hospital after disclosing abuse by a neighbour; the examining doctor, a woman, conducts the medical examination with the child's mother present and records findings as required under Section 164A CrPC, even before the FIR is registered.

A 14-year-old boy in Delhi is referred by the Child Welfare Committee to a district hospital for a medical examination following suspected sexual assault by a school staff member; the examination is carried out by a male doctor with the child's father present.

In a rural area of Rajasthan where no woman doctor is available, the head of the primary health centre nominates a woman nurse to be present during the medical examination of a girl child victim, ensuring compliance with Section 27(4) of the Act.

A paediatrician in Chennai conducts a routine genital examination of a child with a suspected urinary infection with the written consent of both parents; since it is a medically necessary examination undertaken with parental consent, Section 41 excludes this from the offence provisions under sections 3 to 13.

A 9-year-old girl in Kolkata who is unable to communicate is brought by her guardian to a government hospital; in the absence of a parent, a woman nominated by the hospital superintendent is present during the medical examination to satisfy the requirements of the Act.

Following a complaint at a police station in Bengaluru, a Special Juvenile Police Unit officer accompanies a 12-year-old victim to the nearest empanelled hospital where a woman doctor conducts the medical examination and prepares a medico-legal certificate for use in proceedings before the Special Court.
what_it_covers: Physical examination of a child victim of any POCSO offence conducted by a qualified doctor at a government or empanelled hospital in accordance with Section 164A of the CrPC, even before an FIR is registered.
Examination of a girl child victim conducted exclusively by a woman doctor, in the presence of a parent, guardian, trusted person, or a woman nominated by the head of the medical institution.
A formal medical procedure that records injuries, biological material, and physical findings to serve as evidence in proceedings before the Special Court or Children's Court under POCSO.
Medical examination conducted in the presence of a parent or any other person in whom the child reposes trust or confidence, ensuring the child's psychological safety during the procedure.
Examination initiated even without a registered FIR or complaint, recognising the urgency of preserving medical evidence in child sexual abuse cases.
what_it_excludes: Routine medical examinations or treatments conducted by a doctor with the consent of the child's parents or guardian for genuine medical or health purposes, which are expressly excluded from the offence provisions under Section 41 read with sections 3 to 13.

Medical procedures or consultations that do not involve physical examination of the child's body for the purpose of detecting or documenting sexual abuse, such as prescription of medicine for an unrelated illness.

Psychological or psychiatric assessments and counselling sessions conducted by mental health professionals, which fall under a separate category of support services rather than 'medical examination' as governed by Section 27.

Medical examinations conducted without adherence to Section 164A CrPC requirements, such as those done without proper documentation or outside designated medical facilities, which would not satisfy the legal standards set by the Act.
Self-reported or parent-reported accounts of a child's physical condition given to police or welfare officers without a formal clinical examination by a qualified medical professional.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a physical examination qualifies as a 'medical examination' under Section 27 determines whether it generates admissible medico-legal evidence for trial before the Special Court and whether the procedural safeguards of the Act have been fulfilled. Conversely, under Section 41, classifying an examination as a consented medical examination by a qualified doctor exempts it from being prosecuted as penetrative sexual assault, sexual assault, or related offences under sections 3 to 13 of the Act.

definitions.law_name: Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012
definitions.definition: Medical treatment, as used in Section 41 of the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012, refers to any therapeutic, clinical, or health-related procedure or intervention undertaken by a qualified medical professional upon a child for the purpose of diagnosing, treating, or managing a medical condition. Such treatment, when undertaken with the consent of the child's parents or guardian, does not attract the penal provisions of Sections 3 to 13 of the Act, even if it involves acts that would otherwise constitute sexual offences under those sections.
definitions.plain_english: Medical treatment means any proper healthcare procedure carried out by a doctor or medical professional on a child to treat or manage a health condition. If such treatment is done with the permission of the child's parents or guardian, it is not treated as a crime under this law, even if it involves touching private parts of the child's body. This exception exists because legitimate medical care sometimes requires physical examination or contact that would otherwise be prohibited.
real_world_examples: A paediatrician at a government hospital in Mumbai performs a surgical procedure on the genitals of a minor boy to correct a congenital defect (hypospadias repair), with written consent from both parents — this is protected medical treatment under Section 41.

A gynaecologist at a private clinic in Chennai examines and treats a 14-year-old girl for vaginal infection, requiring internal examination, after obtaining the mother's written consent — such treatment falls within the exception and does not constitute sexual assault.

A plastic surgeon at AIIMS, New Delhi, performs a reconstructive procedure on the chest area of a 16-year-old girl following an accident, with guardian's consent — the procedure is shielded from prosecution as lawful medical treatment.

A doctor at a rural primary health centre in Rajasthan administers treatment and conducts a physical examination of a 10-year-old boy to address a urinary tract infection, with both parents present and consenting — this qualifies as protected medical treatment.

An orthopaedic surgeon in Kolkata performs corrective surgery on the lower body of a 12-year-old child after a road accident, involving intimate physical contact, under full parental consent — the procedure is exempted from POCSO offence provisions.

A neonatologist in a Bengaluru NICU performs a circumcision procedure on a newborn male child on medical grounds, with written parental consent — this constitutes medical treatment exempt from the Act's penal provisions.
what_it_covers: Surgical procedures performed by qualified medical professionals on a child's body, including intimate anatomical areas, done with parental or guardian consent for a legitimate health purpose.

Clinical examinations and diagnostic procedures involving physical contact with a child's private parts, conducted by registered medical practitioners in a healthcare setting with appropriate consent.
Emergency or planned therapeutic interventions such as catheterisation, reproductive health treatments, or reconstructive surgeries on minors, where parental or guardian consent has been obtained.
Treatment of infections, congenital conditions, injuries, or diseases in children that require medical professionals to handle or examine private body parts as part of standard clinical care.
Post-assault medical care and treatment administered to a child survivor in a hospital or healthcare facility, with consent of parents or guardian, even if involving intimate examination.
what_it_excludes: Any act performed under the guise of 'medical treatment' by a person who is not a qualified or registered medical professional, which would still attract penal liability under Sections 3 to 13.
Medical examination or treatment conducted without the consent of the child's parents or guardian, which does not receive the benefit of the exemption under Section 41 and may constitute an offence.

Acts performed by medical professionals that go beyond the scope of clinical necessity and are motivated by sexual intent, which would not qualify as genuine medical treatment and would remain punishable.
Procedures or interventions carried out in non-medical settings or for non-therapeutic purposes, even if performed by a person with medical qualifications.
Traditional or faith-based practices involving physical contact with a child's private parts that are not recognised medical procedures, regardless of parental consent.

definitions.law_name: Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012
definitions.definition: As used in the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012, 'mentally ill' carries the meaning assigned to it under clause (l) of section 2 of the Mental Health Act, 1987 (14 of 1987), referring to a person who is in need of treatment by reason of any mental disorder other than mental retardation. In the context of Sections 5 and 9, a child becomes 'mentally ill' when penetrative sexual assault or sexual assault causes or inflicts upon the child a mental condition that renders the child temporarily or permanently unable to perform regular tasks.
definitions.plain_english: 'Mentally ill' refers to a condition where a child suffers from a serious mental disorder as a result of the sexual assault committed on them. This includes any psychological or psychiatric condition caused by the assault that stops the child from carrying out their normal day-to-day activities, either for a limited time or permanently. It does not include intellectual or developmental disabilities like mental retardation. When an assault causes this condition in a child, the crime is treated as a more serious, aggravated offence.
real_world_examples: A child in Delhi who is sexually assaulted by a school staff member subsequently develops severe Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD) and acute psychosis, requiring admission to a government psychiatric facility under the Mental Health Act — rendering the child unable to attend school or communicate, qualifying as 'mentally ill' under this provision.

A minor girl in Mumbai, after repeated sexual abuse by a relative, develops a dissociative identity disorder that prevents her from recognising family members or performing basic self-care activities; a psychiatrist certifies her condition as a mental disorder requiring treatment, attracting the aggravated offence provisions of Section 5.

A young boy in Chennai who is gang sexually assaulted develops severe schizophrenia as a direct consequence of the trauma, as certified by a government hospital psychiatrist, making him unable to perform regular tasks permanently — thereby escalating the offence to aggravated penetrative sexual assault under Section 5(l).

A child in Kolkata is sexually assaulted and subsequently develops major depressive disorder with psychotic features of such severity that she is unable to eat, speak, or interact — confirmed by a registered medical practitioner — triggering the aggravated offence classification under Section 9 of POCSO.

A minor in Hyderabad, subjected to sexual assault by a public servant, develops acute stress disorder evolving into chronic bipolar disorder requiring long-term hospitalisation, certified under the Mental Health Act, 1987, thereby attracting enhanced punishment under the aggravated provisions of POCSO.
what_it_covers: Any mental disorder as defined under clause (l) of Section 2 of the Mental Health Act, 1987, caused to a child as a result of penetrative sexual assault or sexual assault, including conditions like psychosis, schizophrenia, or severe PTSD that require formal psychiatric treatment.

Conditions — whether temporary or permanent — that directly result from the sexual offence and impair the child's ability to carry out regular daily tasks such as eating, communicating, attending school, or basic self-care.

Cases where a child is infected with HIV or another life-threatening disease through the sexual assault that leads to mental illness rendering the child unable to perform regular tasks, as expressly mentioned in Section 5.

Certified psychiatric conditions confirmed by a qualified medical practitioner or psychiatrist, admitted through medical records or expert testimony before the Special Court, establishing the causal link between the assault and the mental illness.
what_it_excludes: Mental retardation or intellectual disabilities, which are expressly excluded from the definition of 'mentally ill' under the Mental Health Act, 1987, and thus fall outside the scope of this term as used in Sections 5 and 9 of POCSO.

Pre-existing mental health conditions that were present in the child before the commission of the offence and are not causally linked to or worsened by the assault — the provision requires the mental illness to be a consequence of the penetrative sexual assault or sexual assault.

Temporary emotional distress, grief, fear, or psychological upset that does not rise to the level of a diagnosable mental disorder requiring treatment under the Mental Health Act, 1987, and does not prevent the child from performing regular tasks.

Physical incapacitation or bodily harm without any associated psychiatric disorder — mere physical disability from the assault does not constitute being 'mentally ill' for the purpose of these sections.
definitions.why_it_matters: If a child is rendered 'mentally ill' as a result of a penetrative sexual assault or sexual assault, the offence is automatically elevated to 'aggravated penetrative sexual assault' under Section 5 or 'aggravated sexual assault' under Section 9, attracting significantly higher minimum and maximum punishments — including rigorous imprisonment of not less than ten years extendable to imprisonment for life under Section 6. This classification also influences the nature of medical examination, rehabilitative support, and the evidentiary requirements before the Special Court.

definitions.law_name: Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012
definitions.definition: In the context of the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012, 'offence' refers to any act or omission constituting penetrative sexual assault, aggravated penetrative sexual assault, sexual assault, aggravated sexual assault, sexual harassment, use of a child for pornographic purposes, or any attempt, abetment, or conspiracy to commit such acts against a child, as defined and punishable under the provisions of this Act. Section 18 specifically provides that any person who attempts to commit an offence under this Act shall be punished with imprisonment of any description provided for that offence for a term which may extend to one-half of the imprisonment for life or, as the case may be, one-half of the longest term of imprisonment provided for that offence, or with fine or with both.
definitions.plain_english: An 'offence' under POCSO means any sexual crime against a child that is listed and punishable under this law — including rape, sexual touching, sexual harassment, and using children in pornography, as well as trying to commit or helping someone else commit such crimes. Even an unsuccessful attempt to commit one of these acts is treated as a separate offence and carries serious punishment. The law covers a wide range of harmful sexual behaviour directed at anyone below 18 years of age.
real_world_examples: A school teacher in Bengaluru who attempts to sexually assault a student but is interrupted before completing the act can still be charged with an 'offence' under Section 18 of POCSO for the attempt itself.

A neighbour in Mumbai who tries to lure a 14-year-old girl into his home with intent to commit sexual assault but is caught at the doorstep has committed an 'offence' (attempt) punishable under POCSO.

An adult in Delhi who downloads and shares child pornographic videos online, even if he does not physically touch any child, has committed an offence under POCSO relating to use of a child for pornographic purposes.
A relative in Chennai who persuades another person to commit penetrative sexual assault on a child has committed the offence of abetment under POCSO, which is equally punishable.

A staff member at a government-run children's shelter home in Kolkata who sexually harasses a child resident by making sexually coloured remarks repeatedly has committed an offence of sexual harassment under POCSO.

Two adults in Hyderabad who plan together to gang-assault a minor and take preparatory steps — such as drugging the child — but are arrested before the assault occurs, can be charged with conspiracy to commit an offence under POCSO.
what_it_covers: Completed acts of penetrative sexual assault, aggravated penetrative sexual assault, sexual assault, aggravated sexual assault, sexual harassment, and use of a child for pornographic purposes as defined under the Act.
An attempt to commit any of the above listed sexual crimes against a child, even where the act is not successfully completed, under Section 18.
Abetment or conspiracy by a person who instigates, aids, or conspires with another to commit any POCSO offence against a child.
Acts committed by persons in positions of authority or trust over a child, such as teachers, police officers, or medical staff, which qualify as aggravated forms of the offence.
Digital or online conduct such as transmitting, distributing or publishing child pornographic material that constitutes an offence under the Act.
what_it_excludes: Acts committed against persons who are 18 years of age or older, which do not fall within the scope of POCSO offences even if sexually criminal in nature.

Civil wrongs or disciplinary violations that do not meet the threshold of any of the enumerated sexual offences under the Act, such as mere inappropriate comments not amounting to sexual harassment as defined in Section 11.
Acts that are lawful medical examinations or medical treatment conducted on a child by qualified medical personnel in appropriate clinical settings.
False complaints or false information filed about POCSO offences, which are separately dealt with under the Act and do not constitute an 'offence' as contemplated in Section 18.
Offences under other laws (e.g., the Indian Penal Code or IT Act) that relate to adults or do not involve the specific sexual conduct against children enumerated under POCSO.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act qualifies as an 'offence' under POCSO determines whether the mandatory minimum sentences, special court procedures, and child-sensitive evidentiary rules of the Act are triggered; it also governs whether an attempt or abetment is independently punishable under Section 18, attracting up to half the maximum imprisonment prescribed for the completed offence. The classification directly impacts bail eligibility, the burden of proof provisions, and the obligation of Special Courts and Special Public Prosecutors to handle the case.

definitions.law_name: Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012
definitions.definition: An 'offense' under the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012, refers to any act or omission constituting a criminal wrong as defined and penalised under this Act, including but not limited to penetrative sexual assault, sexual assault, sexual harassment, and child pornography committed against a child, as well as the failure to report or record such acts as mandated under Sections 19 and 20 of the Act.
definitions.plain_english: An 'offense' means any wrongful act against a child that is made punishable under the POCSO Act, such as sexual assault, harassment, or exploitation of children. It also includes the wrongful failure to report or document such acts when legally required to do so. Essentially, it covers both the harmful acts themselves and certain failures to act that the law treats as criminal.
real_world_examples: A schoolteacher in Mumbai witnesses a colleague inappropriately touching a student but does not report it to the police or authorities — the teacher's failure to report constitutes an offense under Section 21 of POCSO.

The principal of a residential school in Delhi becomes aware that a warden has been sexually harassing students but deliberately avoids recording or reporting the matter to protect the school's reputation — this omission is an offense punishable under Section 21.

A hospital staff member in Chennai who examines a child showing signs of sexual abuse fails to report the suspected offense to the Special Juvenile Police Unit or local police — this failure to report is an offense under the Act.

A child care institution manager in Kolkata learns from a subordinate staff member that a child in the facility has been subjected to penetrative sexual assault but takes no steps to report it to the authorities — the manager commits an offense under Section 21(2) attracting imprisonment up to one year and fine.

A neighbour in Hyderabad who witnesses an act of sexual harassment against a minor but knowingly omits to inform the police or any authority as required under Section 19 commits an offense under Section 21(1) of the POCSO Act.
what_it_covers: Any act of penetrative sexual assault, sexual assault, sexual harassment, or use of a child for pornographic purposes as defined and penalised under the POCSO Act.
The failure by any person to report the commission of a sexual offense against a child as mandated under Section 19(1) of the Act.
The failure by a person in charge of a company or institution to report an offense committed by a subordinate under their control against a child.
The failure by a police officer or special unit to record an offense as required under Section 19(2) of the Act.
Abetment of, attempt to commit, or conspiracy to commit any of the offenses enumerated under the POCSO Act.
what_it_excludes: A child who fails to report an offense — Section 21(3) explicitly exempts children from the reporting obligation and its penal consequences.

Acts or omissions that do not fall within the specific categories of sexual offenses or reporting failures enumerated under the POCSO Act — general civil wrongs or violations under other laws are not covered.
Failure to report an offense that was not reasonably known or discoverable by the person — inadvertent ignorance without culpable mental state may fall outside the scope of this provision.
Offenses committed against adults — the Act exclusively governs offenses against children (persons below 18 years of age).
Procedural or administrative irregularities by officials that do not amount to a deliberate failure to report or record under Sections 19 or 20.
definitions.why_it_matters: The definition of 'offense' under Section 21 directly determines criminal liability — it triggers mandatory reporting duties and imposes imprisonment and fines on those who fail to report or record sexual offenses against children. Whether an act qualifies as an 'offense' under this Act governs cognizance by the Special Court, prosecution under POCSO, and the protective and punitive mechanisms available to the State and the child victim.

definitions.law_name: Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012
definitions.definition: A person is said to commit 'penetrative sexual assault' if he penetrates his penis, to any extent, into the vagina, mouth, urethra or anus of a child or makes the child to do so with him or any other person; or inserts, to any extent, any object or a part of the body, not being the penis, into the vagina, the urethra or anus of the child or makes the child to do so with him or any other person; or manipulates any part of the body of the child so as to cause penetration into the vagina, urethra, anus or any part of body of the child or makes the child to do so with him or any other person; or applies his mouth to the penis, vagina, anus, urethra of the child or makes the child to do so to such person or any other person.
definitions.plain_english: Penetrative sexual assault means any act where an adult forces or causes sexual penetration involving a child under 18 years of age. This includes using body parts or objects to penetrate a child's private parts, or using one's mouth on a child's genitals. It also covers situations where the offender forces the child to perform such acts on the offender or on another person.
real_world_examples: A male relative in a Delhi household forcibly penetrates a 10-year-old girl's vagina with his penis — this constitutes penetrative sexual assault under Section 3(a) of POCSO.

A school teacher in Mumbai inserts his finger into the anus of a 12-year-old male student during a private session after class — this falls under Section 3(b) as insertion of a body part other than the penis.

An adult neighbour in Chennai uses a foreign object such as a bottle to penetrate the vagina of a 14-year-old girl — this constitutes penetrative sexual assault under Section 3(b) as insertion of an object.

A domestic worker in Kolkata forces a 9-year-old child to perform oral sex on him, i.e., applying the child's mouth to his penis — this is covered under Section 3(d) as the child is made to apply her or his mouth to the offender's genitalia.

A man in Hyderabad manipulates a 7-year-old child's body by pressing and directing the child's limb so as to cause penetration into the child's own anus — this constitutes penetrative sexual assault under Section 3(c) through body manipulation.
An adult male in Bengaluru applies his mouth to the vagina of a 13-year-old girl — this is explicitly covered under Section 3(d) as oral contact with the child's genitalia.
what_it_covers: Penile penetration to any extent into the vagina, mouth, urethra or anus of a child, whether committed by the accused directly or by forcing the child to perform it on him or another person.
Insertion of any object or any non-penile body part (such as fingers, hands or other limbs) into the vagina, urethra or anus of the child, or compelling the child to perform the same.

Body manipulation by the offender that results in penetration into the vagina, urethra, anus or any part of the child's body, including making the child perform such manipulation on the accused or another person.

Oral-genital contact, including applying the offender's mouth to the child's penis, vagina, anus or urethra, or compelling the child to apply their mouth to the genitalia of the accused or any other person.
Acts committed by any person regardless of gender of the offender, since the Act's presumption and punishment provisions apply broadly.
what_it_excludes: Non-penetrative sexual touching or physical contact with a child's body that does not involve any form of penetration — such acts may constitute 'sexual assault' under Section 7 but not penetrative sexual assault.
Sexual harassment of a child involving words, gestures, electronic communication or exhibitionism, which falls under Section 11 as 'sexual harassment' and not penetrative sexual assault.
Penetrative acts committed between persons above 18 years of age, as the definition is exclusively applicable where the victim is a child, i.e., a person below 18 years of age.

Production, storage or distribution of child pornography involving depictions of penetrative acts, which is separately governed under Section 14 and 15 of the Act and does not constitute penetrative sexual assault in itself.

Acts that are part of legitimate medical examination or medical treatment conducted in accordance with law and professional standards, which are excluded from the purview of criminal liability under the Act.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act qualifies as 'penetrative sexual assault' under Section 3 directly determines whether the accused is liable for punishment under Section 4 (minimum 10 years, extendable to life imprisonment) or Section 6 (minimum 20 years to life, if aggravated), as opposed to the lesser offence of sexual assault under Section 7; it also serves as the predicate offence for aggravated penetrative sexual assault under Section 5 and triggers the presumption of guilt under Section 29 of the Act.

definitions.definition: Physical contact, as used in Section 7 of the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012, refers to any act involving direct bodily touching of a child or causing a child to touch another person, done with sexual intent, without penetration. It encompasses touching of the vagina, penis, anus, or breast of the child by the offender, or making the child touch those body parts of the offender or any other person, as well as any other act involving bodily contact with sexual intent that does not amount to penetrative sexual assault.
definitions.plain_english: Physical contact means when an adult or another person deliberately touches a child's private parts (or makes the child touch theirs) in a sexual way, without any penetration occurring. It includes any direct body-to-body touching done with a sexual motive. This can happen through clothing or directly on the skin. It is different from more severe forms of assault because it does not involve penetration.
real_world_examples: A school teacher in Mumbai touches a student's chest or groin area over the uniform while alone in the classroom, claiming it was accidental, but the act is done with sexual intent.
A relative visiting a family home in Chennai forces a young child to touch the relative's genital area during a private moment, which constitutes physical contact under Section 7.
A neighbour in Delhi repeatedly pats or strokes a child's buttocks under the pretext of playing or showing affection, but does so with sexual intent and without the child's understanding of the act.
A tutor in Kolkata brushes his hand against a teenage student's breast or groin area during a home tuition session, which amounts to sexual assault through physical contact under POCSO.
An unknown person on a crowded local train in Bengaluru deliberately touches the private parts of a minor travelling alone, constituting physical contact with sexual intent under the Act.
what_it_covers: Touching the vagina, penis, anus, or breast of a child by the offender with sexual intent, whether over or under clothing.
Making a child touch the vagina, penis, anus, or breast of the offender or any third person with sexual intent.

Any other act involving direct bodily contact between the offender and the child that is done with sexual intent and does not involve penetration, such as rubbing, pressing, or stroking private or sensitive body parts.
Instances where the touching is brief or momentary but is accompanied by demonstrable sexual intent on the part of the accused.
Situations where a child is made to participate in the physical contact through force, coercion, inducement, or manipulation.
what_it_excludes: Acts involving penetration of the vagina, mouth, urethra, or anus by a body part or object, which fall under penetrative sexual assault under Section 3 of the Act.
Incidental or accidental physical contact with a child that occurs without any sexual intent, such as a doctor conducting a routine medical examination.

Non-contact sexual offences such as displaying pornographic material to a child, making a child exhibit their body, or sexually harassing a child through words, gestures, or electronic communication without physical touching.
Acts of aggravated sexual assault which are governed separately under Sections 9 and 10 of the Act, although those provisions build upon this definition.
Physical contact between children of similar age in consensual play contexts where no sexual intent is established or proven.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act constitutes 'physical contact' under Section 7 determines if the accused is liable for sexual assault, which is punishable with imprisonment of not less than three years and up to five years along with a fine under Section 8 of the Act. The presence or absence of sexual intent accompanying the physical contact is decisive in distinguishing a criminal offence from an innocent or medical act, thereby triggering or blocking prosecution and mandatory reporting obligations under POCSO.

definitions.definition: A police officer, for the purposes of this Act, refers to any member of a police force appointed under any law for the time being in force, who is recognised or identifiable as such, and includes any person acting in the capacity of a police officer within the limits of a police station, its premises, any station house, or in the course of official duties. The term is used contextually in Sections 5 and 9 to identify the status of the perpetrator as an aggravating circumstance, and in Sections 21 and 24 to impose specific duties and procedural obligations on such officers.
definitions.plain_english: A police officer is any person who is a member of the police force in India — someone who wears a uniform, holds a police rank, or is known to the public as a cop. Under this law, a police officer has special duties, like reporting crimes against children, and also faces harsher punishment if they themselves commit a sexual offence against a child. The law treats crimes by police officers as more serious because children and families are expected to trust them.
