definitions.law_name: Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012
definitions.definition: The term 'pornographic' is not separately defined in the Act but is used contextually to describe content, purposes, or acts involving the sexual exploitation or indecent representation of a child through any form of media, including showing objects to a child for pornographic purposes or enticing a child for pornographic purposes, as used in Section 11. It encompasses any material, act, or intent directed at the sexual gratification of a person through the depiction or involvement of a child.
definitions.plain_english: The word 'pornographic' refers to anything related to creating, showing, or using sexual content that involves a child. This includes showing a child sexually explicit objects or images, or trying to involve a child in sexual content for someone else's gratification. Under this law, even the intent to use something pornographic against a child is enough to be considered an offence.
real_world_examples: A person in Mumbai shows a minor obscene images on a mobile phone under the pretext of 'education' to sexually harass the child — this constitutes showing an object for pornographic purposes under Section 11.
An adult in Delhi attempts to lure a child with money or gifts to pose for photographs intended for sexual content — this amounts to enticing a child for pornographic purposes under Section 11.

A school teacher in Chennai uses a projector to display sexually explicit material to a student as part of alleged 'awareness', with sexual intent — this qualifies as showing objects to a child for pornographic purposes.

A person in Kolkata sends a WhatsApp message with a sexually explicit image to a 12-year-old with the intent that the child views it — this is an act of sexual harassment involving pornographic material under Section 11.

An individual in Bengaluru repeatedly sends obscene videos via social media to a minor, intending to arouse the child or gratify themselves — this constitutes pornographic-purpose contact under Section 11.
what_it_covers: Showing any sexually explicit image, video, or object to a child with sexual intent, whether through physical or digital means.
Enticing or luring a child to participate in, pose for, or be involved in the creation of sexually explicit content.
Using any form of media — print, electronic, digital, or internet — to expose a child to sexually explicit material for the purpose of sexual gratification.
Any gesture, act, or communication directed at a child that is intended to serve pornographic purposes, including simulated or real depictions.
Content involving the indecent or obscene representation of a child's body or sexual acts, even if not distributed publicly.
what_it_excludes: Age-appropriate, medically accurate sexual education material presented without sexual intent by qualified professionals in a school or clinical setting.
Bona fide depictions of a child's body in a medical, legal, or documentary context without any element of sexual gratification or intent.
Material stored or reported solely for the purpose of evidence in legal proceedings or reporting to designated authorities under Section 15.
Artistic or cultural representations of children that do not involve indecency, obscenity, or sexual gratification.
Incidental exposure of a child to adult-oriented content where there is no sexual intent directed at or involving the child.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act qualifies as 'pornographic' determines whether an accused is liable for sexual harassment under Section 11 or for use of a child for pornographic purposes under Sections 13 and 14, which carry mandatory minimum imprisonment of five years. It also triggers obligations under Section 15 regarding storage, possession, and reporting of such material to designated authorities.

definitions.law_name: Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012
definitions.definition: Pornographic material involving a child means any material in any form — including print, electronic, digital, or any other medium — that uses a child for the purposes of sexual gratification, encompassing representation of sexual organs of a child, depiction of a child engaged in real or simulated sexual acts (with or without penetration), or the indecent or obscene representation of a child, as construed from Section 13 read with Section 15 of this Act.
definitions.plain_english: Pornographic material, as used in this law, means any content — whether a photo, video, printed image, digital file, or any other format — that shows a child in a sexual way. This includes images or videos of a child's private parts, a child performing or appearing to perform sexual acts, or any content that depicts a child in an indecent or obscene manner. The content qualifies regardless of whether it was made for personal viewing or for sharing with others.
real_world_examples: A person in Mumbai downloads and stores video files on his laptop showing minors engaged in sexual acts, obtained from a dark web forum, without deleting or reporting them — this constitutes possession of pornographic material involving a child under Section 15.

A photographer in Delhi captures obscene images of a child and stores them on a pen drive, later intending to sell them to an online network — such stored images constitute pornographic material for commercial purpose under Section 15(3).

A WhatsApp group in Chennai is used to circulate photographs showing the private parts of minors; each member who stores and forwards such images is in possession of pornographic material involving a child and liable under Section 15(2).

An NGO worker in Bengaluru discovers child sexual abuse material on a seized device during field work and retains it temporarily solely to produce it as evidence before the Special Court — this retention falls within the statutory exception and does not attract punishment under Section 15.

A school teacher in Kolkata secretly records a student in a state of undress using a mobile phone and stores the footage — the stored recording constitutes pornographic material involving a child, triggering liability under Section 15.

An advertisement production house in Hyderabad produces a digital advertisement that displays minors in an obscene and sexualised manner for an online platform; the digital files stored at the production house qualify as pornographic material involving a child.
what_it_covers: Photographs, videos, GIFs, or digital files depicting a child's sexual organs or engaged in sexual activity, whether real or simulated.
Printed material such as magazines, pamphlets, or photographs that indecently or obscenely represent a child for purposes of sexual gratification.
Content transmitted or stored across electronic media — including mobile phones, computers, cloud storage, pen drives, or internet platforms — that depicts a child in a sexual or obscene manner.
Animated or computer-generated images and representations that depict a child in a sexually explicit or indecent manner.
Audio-visual recordings — including those made without the child's knowledge — that capture a child in a state of undress or engaged in sexual acts.
what_it_excludes: Medical or clinical images of a child's body recorded strictly for bona fide medical examination or medical treatment purposes, with no element of sexual gratification.
Educational or anatomical content prepared by recognised institutions for child health awareness that does not depict children in an indecent or sexually gratifying manner.

Material retained exclusively as evidence for use in court proceedings or for the purpose of reporting to the designated authority as prescribed under Section 15, provided it is not stored beyond that necessity.

Lawful journalism or documentary content depicting child abuse in a non-obscene, non-gratifying manner solely for the purpose of raising awareness or news reporting, where no sexual representation is involved.
General entertainment content — such as films certified by the Central Board of Film Certification — that features child actors in age-appropriate, non-sexual roles.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether stored or possessed material qualifies as 'pornographic material involving a child' directly determines criminal liability under Section 15, which prescribes a graded set of punishments ranging from fines for mere failure to delete or report, to imprisonment up to three years for possession with intent to transmit, and imprisonment of three to seven years for commercial possession — distinguishing among these offences hinges entirely on whether the material meets this definition. The definition also triggers mandatory reporting obligations and the right of authorities to prescribe rules for deletion, destruction, and reporting under Section 45.

definitions.definition: Every person appointed as a Special Public Prosecutor under section 32 shall be deemed to be a Public Prosecutor within the meaning of clause (u) of section 2 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, and the person conducting a prosecution before a Special Court shall be deemed to be a Public Prosecutor for the purposes of the provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 as applied to proceedings before a Special Court.
definitions.plain_english: A Public Prosecutor, in the context of POCSO, is a legally qualified advocate appointed by the State Government to represent the State and the child victim in criminal cases heard before a Special Court. This person is responsible for presenting the prosecution's case against the accused who is charged with offences under the Act. They are treated as a Public Prosecutor under the general criminal procedure law of India and must have at least seven years of experience as an advocate.
real_world_examples: In a case in Mumbai where a school teacher is accused of sexually assaulting a student, the Maharashtra State Government appoints an experienced advocate as Special Public Prosecutor to argue the case before the designated POCSO Special Court in the city.

In Delhi, after a police chargesheet is filed against a neighbour for penetrative sexual assault of a minor girl, the Special Public Prosecutor appointed under POCSO conducts the examination-in-chief of the child witness through the Special Court, ensuring the child is not directly questioned by the defence.

In a Bengaluru case involving online sexual exploitation of a child, the State Government-appointed Public Prosecutor applies for denial of bail to the accused before the Special Court, invoking the provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure as made applicable under Section 31 of POCSO.

In a rural district of Uttar Pradesh, where a local advocate with over seven years of practice is notified by the State Government via Official Gazette as Special Public Prosecutor for the POCSO Special Court, that advocate then represents the State in all child sexual offence trials in that district.

During a trial in Chennai involving aggravated sexual assault by a relative, the Special Public Prosecutor argues for enhanced compensation to be awarded to the child victim under Section 33 of POCSO, as part of the prosecution's closing submissions before the Special Court.

Any person conducting prosecution before a Special Court under POCSO, who is deemed to be a Public Prosecutor for the purposes of applying Code of Criminal Procedure provisions, including those relating to bail and bonds.

A Special Public Prosecutor appointed under Section 32 who is granted all rights and duties of a Public Prosecutor as defined under clause (u) of Section 2 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, including cross-examination rights and bail applications.
A Public Prosecutor from the regular cadre of government prosecutors who is specifically designated and notified by the State Government to handle POCSO cases before a Special Court.

definitions.definition: The term 'public servant' is not independently defined in the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012; it carries the meaning assigned to it under Section 21 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (now Section 2(60) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023), encompassing every person in the service or pay of the Government, or remunerated by fees or commissions for the performance of any public duty by the Government. As used in Sections 5 and 9 of POCSO, a public servant who commits penetrative sexual assault or sexual assault on a child is deemed to have committed aggravated forms of those offences.
definitions.plain_english: A 'public servant' is anyone who works for the government or performs a duty on behalf of the government — such as a government school teacher, a municipal worker, a judicial officer, or a government hospital employee. Under the POCSO Act, if such a person sexually assaults a child, the law treats it as a more serious crime than if an ordinary private individual had done it. This is because public servants are trusted with authority and power, and abusing that trust against a child is treated very harshly.
real_world_examples: A government school teacher employed by a state education board who sexually assaults a student would be prosecuted under the aggravated penetrative sexual assault provision of Section 5 of POCSO, as he is a public servant.

A municipal corporation sanitation worker (a public servant) who commits sexual assault on a child in a government-maintained area can be charged under Section 9 of POCSO for aggravated sexual assault.

A judicial clerk or court officer attached to a district court who sexually assaults a child witness brought to the court premises would face aggravated charges under POCSO by virtue of being a public servant.

A government-employed Anganwadi worker under the Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS) scheme who commits sexual assault on a child enrolled in her centre would be liable under Section 9 of POCSO as a public servant.

A Block Development Officer (BDO) who abuses his position and sexually assaults a child from a beneficiary family during a field visit would be charged under POCSO's aggravated assault provisions as a public servant.

A public sector undertaking (PSU) employee designated with public duties, such as a railway employee who assaults a child traveller, may be treated as a public servant for the purposes of attracting aggravated liability under POCSO.
what_it_covers: Government school teachers, principals, and education department employees who interact with children in their official capacity.
Judicial officers, court staff, magistrates, and clerks who are appointed by or under the authority of the State or Central Government.
Employees of government hospitals, public health centres, Anganwadi centres, and other state-run welfare institutions who work with or around children.
Municipal and panchayat-level officials, including those employed under local self-government bodies exercising public duties.
Officers and staff of public sector undertakings (PSUs) and statutory bodies who are remunerated for performing a public duty and have access to children.
Child Welfare Officers, probation officers, and social welfare department employees deployed in government-run observation homes or care institutions.
what_it_excludes: Private school teachers or staff employed solely by unaided private educational institutions with no government appointment or remuneration — they may fall under other categories (e.g., management/staff of educational institution) but not specifically as public servants.

Police officers and members of armed forces or security forces, who are separately enumerated as distinct aggravating categories in Sections 5 and 9 and are not subsumed under the 'public servant' sub-clause.
NGO workers or staff of private charitable organisations, even if they receive government grants, as they are not in the direct service or pay of the Government in the sense of Section 21 IPC.
Contractual or daily-wage private labourers working on government projects who do not perform any public duty or exercise any governmental authority.

Members of the management or staff of privately managed jails, hospitals, or educational institutions, who are covered under separate sub-clauses in Sections 5 and 9 rather than the public servant clause.
definitions.why_it_matters: When a perpetrator qualifies as a 'public servant' under Sections 5 or 9 of POCSO, the offence is automatically elevated to 'aggravated penetrative sexual assault' or 'aggravated sexual assault', attracting a minimum imprisonment of ten years extendable to life imprisonment (Section 6) or a minimum of five years extendable to seven years (Section 10), as opposed to the lower penalties for basic offences — the classification thus directly determines the severity of the sentence imposed by the Special Court.

definitions.definition: 'Religious institution' shall have the same meaning as assigned to it in the Religious Institutions (Prevention of Misuse) Act, 1988 (41 of 1988), which refers to a place of public religious worship or a religious body or organisation established and maintained for religious purposes.
definitions.plain_english: A religious institution is any organised place or body set up for religious worship or religious purposes — such as a temple, mosque, church, gurudwara, monastery, or religious school. The POCSO Act borrows this meaning from an older law that was designed to prevent misuse of such institutions. It includes both the physical premises and the managing body or organisation behind them.
real_world_examples: A priest at a well-known temple in Tirupati who commits sexual assault on a child devotee within the temple complex — the institution qualifies as a religious institution, making the offence 'aggravated' under Section 5.

A madrasa attached to a mosque in Lucknow where a teacher who is part of the mosque management commits penetrative sexual assault on a child student — the madrasa-mosque complex is a religious institution for the purposes of POCSO.

A Christian missionary school run by a diocese in Shillong, where a staff member commits sexual assault on a child enrolled in the institution — since the school is managed by a religious body, it falls under the definition of a religious institution.

A gurudwara-run residential sevadal camp in Amritsar where a caretaker on the management staff of the gurudwara committee sexually assaults a child participant — the gurudwara trust is a religious institution under POCSO.

A Hindu math (monastery) in Udupi that runs a free residential school (gurukul) for children, where the head of the math commits sexual assault on a child resident — the math qualifies as a religious institution, triggering aggravated offence provisions.
what_it_covers: Temples, mosques, churches, gurudwaras, synagogues, and other places of public religious worship registered or functioning as religious institutions under Indian law.

Religious organisations, trusts, and bodies established and maintained for religious purposes, including those that operate residential schools, ashrams, orphanages, or care homes for children under their religious management.

The staff and management personnel of such institutions — including priests, clerics, administrators, caretakers, and teachers employed or authorised by the religious body — when they commit offences on children within the institution's premises.
Monasteries, mutts, dargahs, and similar religious residential establishments where children may reside or attend for religious education.
what_it_excludes: Private homes or residences of religious figures (e.g., a priest's personal house) that are not formally part of or managed by a religious institution.
Secular educational institutions or schools that have no organisational or managerial link to any religious body, even if they occasionally conduct religious activities or have a religious name.

Non-governmental organisations or charitable trusts that operate on a non-religious basis, even if founded by persons of a particular faith, provided they are not established and maintained for religious purposes.

Government-run facilities such as observation homes, remand homes, or government hospitals, which are separately covered under other clauses of Section 5 and are not 'religious institutions' within the meaning of this definition.
definitions.why_it_matters: When an accused is on the management or staff of a religious institution and commits penetrative sexual assault or sexual assault on a child within that institution, the offence is elevated to 'aggravated penetrative sexual assault' under Section 5 or 'aggravated sexual assault' under Section 9, attracting significantly harsher minimum and maximum punishments. This classification directly determines whether the enhanced sentencing provisions apply and may influence bail eligibility and the gravity of charges framed by the Special Court.

definitions.definition: 'Armed forces or security forces' means armed forces of the Union or security forces or police forces, as specified in the Schedule. In the context of Section 9, 'security forces' refers to those security or police forces enumerated in the Schedule to the Act, whose members are subject to heightened criminal liability when they commit sexual assault on a child.
definitions.plain_english: Security forces are organised government forces such as paramilitary units, central armed police forces, and state police forces that are listed in the Schedule attached to the POCSO Act. A member of any such force who sexually assaults a child is treated more seriously by the law than an ordinary person committing the same act. This is because these personnel are in positions of authority and public trust, making their offences more harmful and blameworthy.
real_world_examples: A CRPF (Central Reserve Police Force) jawan deployed in Chhattisgarh commits sexual assault on a child living in a village within his operational area — he is covered under 'security forces' and the offence is treated as aggravated sexual assault under Section 9.

A BSF (Border Security Force) constable posted at a border checkpoint in Rajasthan sexually assaults a minor — because BSF is listed in the Schedule, he is a member of security forces under POCSO and faces enhanced punishment.

A member of the CISF (Central Industrial Security Force) guarding a public sector undertaking in Maharashtra sexually assaults a child worker on the premises — CISF being a scheduled security force, the offence qualifies as aggravated sexual assault.

A state Armed Police Battalion personnel in Uttar Pradesh, while on duty in a riot-affected area, commits sexual assault on a child — since state armed police forces are included in the Schedule, this triggers the aggravated offence provisions under Section 9.

An Indo-Tibetan Border Police (ITBP) officer in Uttarakhand sexually assaults a child in the course of conducting a search operation — ITBP being a Union security force listed in the Schedule, the act constitutes aggravated sexual assault under POCSO.
what_it_covers: Central armed police forces of the Union listed in the Schedule, such as CRPF, BSF, CISF, ITBP, and SSB, whose members are treated as security forces under POCSO.
State police forces and state armed police battalions that are specifically enumerated in the Schedule to the Act, making their personnel subject to aggravated offence provisions.

Any member of such a scheduled security or police force who commits sexual assault on a child whether in the course of their duties, within their area of deployment, or while identified as a member of that force.
what_it_excludes: Private security guards or personnel employed by private security agencies, who are not government security forces and are not listed in the Schedule.
Intelligence agency personnel such as RAW or IB officers who are not part of any force listed in the Schedule to the Act.
Civilian government employees or public servants who are not members of any armed, paramilitary, or police force listed in the Schedule, even if they work alongside security forces.

This classification also affects investigation protocols, Special Court proceedings, and the sentencing framework applicable to the accused.

definitions.law_name: Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012
definitions.definition: 'Sexual assault' has the same meaning as assigned to it in section 7, which provides that a person is said to commit sexual assault if, with sexual intent, he touches the vagina, penis, anus or breast of the child or makes the child touch the vagina, penis, anus or breast of such person or any other person, or does any other act with sexual intent which involves physical contact without penetration.
definitions.plain_english: Sexual assault under this law means any intentional physical touching of a child's private body parts — or making a child touch someone else's private parts — without penetration and with a sexual purpose. It covers direct skin-to-skin contact as well as contact through clothing or other material. It is distinct from penetrative sexual assault, which involves insertion, and is a serious criminal offence regardless of the gender of the child or the accused.
real_world_examples: A school teacher in Chennai repeatedly touches a 10-year-old student's chest over the uniform during after-school tuition sessions, with clear sexual intent, but without any penetration — this constitutes sexual assault under the Act.

A neighbour in a Mumbai chawl grabs a 13-year-old girl's buttocks while passing her in a corridor, intending sexual gratification — this non-penetrative intentional touching with sexual intent amounts to sexual assault.

An auto-rickshaw driver in Delhi, while giving a ride to a 14-year-old boy, places his hand on the child's groin area over the clothing with sexual intent — this qualifies as sexual assault even though no skin-to-skin contact occurred.

A domestic worker's employer in Kolkata forces a 12-year-old child domestic worker to touch the employer's genitals — the act of making the child touch the accused's private parts with sexual intent constitutes sexual assault.

A cricket coach in Pune repeatedly pats a 15-year-old male student on the groin area under the pretext of checking protective gear, the pattern and context establishing sexual intent — this constitutes sexual assault under the Act.

A relative visiting a home in Hyderabad kisses a 9-year-old child on the lips and touches the child's private parts over clothes during a family gathering — this physical contact with sexual intent, absent penetration, amounts to sexual assault.
what_it_covers: Intentional touching of a child's vagina, penis, anus or breast by the accused with sexual intent, whether skin-to-skin or over clothing.
Acts where the accused makes or compels the child to touch the accused's or any third person's vagina, penis, anus or breast with sexual intent.
Any other act involving physical contact with a child — not amounting to penetration — carried out with sexual intent, such as rubbing, fondling or pressing body parts.
Touching through fabric, clothing or other material where sexual intent is established, as courts have held that skin-to-skin contact is not a prerequisite.
Acts committed against a child of any gender by a person of any gender, given the gender-neutral framing of the provision.
what_it_excludes: Penetrative acts involving insertion of the penis, any object, or body part into orifices of the child — these are governed separately as 'penetrative sexual assault' under section 3.

Non-contact sexual acts such as showing pornography to a child, exhibitionism or making sexually explicit remarks — these may constitute 'sexual harassment' under section 11 but do not fall within sexual assault.

Accidental or incidental physical contact with a child's body that lacks any sexual intent, such as a doctor's clinical examination or a parent's routine caregiving, even if intimate body parts are involved.
Conduct that meets the higher threshold of 'aggravated sexual assault' under section 9, which is a distinct and more serious category attracting enhanced punishment under section 10.
Production, storage or distribution of child pornography, which is a separate offence under section 14 and 15, and does not require physical contact with the child.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act qualifies as 'sexual assault' under section 7 determines whether the accused is liable for punishment under section 8 (minimum 3 years, extendable to 5 years, plus fine) or, in aggravated circumstances under section 9, for enhanced punishment under section 10; it also activates the presumption of guilt under section 29 once penetration or sexual assault is alleged, shifting the burden to the accused to prove innocence.

definitions.definition: Sexual intent is not formally defined in the Act but is used as the operative mental element in Sections 7 and 11. It refers to the subjective purpose or motive of a sexual nature with which a person touches a child, makes a child touch another, or engages in conduct such as utterances, gestures, exhibition of objects, following, threatening, or enticement directed at a child. Any question involving sexual intent shall be a question of fact.
definitions.plain_english: Sexual intent means that a person is doing something because they want to use it for a sexual purpose involving a child. It is the inner motive or purpose — the reason why someone touches a child, says something, shows something, or follows a child — and that reason must be sexual in nature. Courts decide whether sexual intent existed by looking at all the facts and circumstances of each case, not by applying a fixed rule.
real_world_examples: A school van driver in Mumbai repeatedly touches the thighs of a child passenger while claiming it is accidental; the court examines the frequency, context, and manner of touching to determine whether sexual intent was present under Section 7.

A neighbour in Delhi calls out sexual remarks to a young girl passing by, and then shows her an obscene image on his mobile phone; the court assesses whether these acts were committed with sexual intent to establish sexual harassment under Section 11.

A tuition teacher in Chennai repeatedly messages a 13-year-old student through WhatsApp asking her to share photographs of her body, threatening to spread fabricated images of her if she refuses; the pattern of contact and the nature of the threat are examined to infer sexual intent under Section 11.

During a medical check-up camp in a rural district of Rajasthan, a person who is not a licensed medical professional touches the private parts of a child without any legitimate medical purpose; the absence of medical justification and the manner of touch are used by the court to determine the presence of sexual intent under Section 7.

A relative at a family function in Kolkata pulls a child onto his lap and presses his body against the child while the child is visibly uncomfortable; the court considers the body language, the setting, and the reaction of the child to infer whether the act was committed with sexual intent.

A shopkeeper in Hyderabad lures a child with chocolates and gifts and then shows the child pornographic content on a tablet, which the court uses to assess sexual intent in the context of enticement under Section 11.
what_it_covers: A deliberate touch of a child's private parts motivated by the accused's sexual gratification or arousal, even if no penetration occurs, making it sexual assault under Section 7.

Persistent online or electronic contact with a child — such as repeated messaging, video calls, or following on social media — when the purpose behind such contact is sexual in nature, covered under Section 11.
Showing a child pornographic material, making sexual gestures toward a child, or uttering sexual words intended to be heard by the child, where the actor's motive is sexual, covered under Section 11.
Threatening to use real or fabricated depictions of a child's body in any media with the underlying motive of sexual coercion or gratification, covered under Section 11.
Enticing a child with gifts, money, or gratification for pornographic purposes, where the purpose of the inducement is sexual, covered under Section 11.
what_it_excludes: Legitimate medical examinations or medical treatment of a child carried out by a licensed medical professional in a proper clinical setting, where there is no sexual motive behind the physical contact.

Routine and culturally accepted non-sexual physical contact such as a parent bathing a young child, a teacher placing a hand on a child's shoulder for guidance, or a caregiver changing an infant's clothes, where no sexual purpose is present.
Accidental or unintentional physical contact with a child in crowded public spaces such as buses or markets, where there is no subjective sexual motive behind the contact.
Educational or awareness content about child safety, sex education, or health provided by authorised teachers or counsellors in a school setting without any sexual intent toward the child.
definitions.why_it_matters: The presence of sexual intent is the decisive threshold element that elevates otherwise ordinary physical contact or communication into the criminal offences of sexual assault under Section 7 and sexual harassment under Section 11 of POCSO; without establishing sexual intent, the prosecution cannot secure a conviction under these provisions. Because it is expressly a question of fact, courts must examine the totality of circumstances — including the nature of the act, the relationship between the parties, the setting, and the conduct of the accused — to determine guilt, which directly affects sentencing, mandatory reporting obligations, and the child's entitlement to protection and support services under the Act.

definitions.definition: "shared household" means a household where the person charged with the offence lives or has lived at any time in a domestic relationship with the child.
definitions.plain_english: A shared household is any home where the accused person currently lives or has lived together with the child at some point, as part of a domestic relationship. This includes family homes, rented accommodations, or any dwelling where the accused and child cohabited under a recognised domestic bond. It does not require that the accused and child live there at the same time as the offence — past cohabitation is sufficient.
real_world_examples: A stepfather who lives in the same house as his stepdaughter in Mumbai commits sexual assault on her — their home qualifies as a shared household, making the offence aggravated penetrative sexual assault under Section 5.

An uncle in Delhi who has been living with his nephew in the same flat for several months commits a sexual offence — the flat is a shared household because they have a domestic relationship and cohabit.

A live-in partner of a child's mother in Chennai, who resides in the family home, sexually assaults the child — the home is considered a shared household as the accused has a domestic relationship with the child's parent and lives there.

A paternal grandfather in Kolkata who previously lived with his grandchildren for years but has since moved out commits an offence against the child — the earlier home can still qualify as a shared household because he 'has lived' there in a domestic relationship with the child at any time in the past.

A female teacher who is a live-in caretaker residing in the same household as the child in a rural Rajasthan setting commits an offence — the dwelling qualifies as a shared household given the domestic relationship and cohabitation.
A foster parent in Pune residing in the same home as a foster child commits sexual assault — since foster care creates a domestic relationship, the home is a shared household under POCSO.
what_it_covers: A home where the accused currently lives together with the child in a domestic relationship, such as a parent, stepparent, or guardian residing with the child.
A household where the accused formerly resided with the child at any past point in time under a domestic relationship, even if the accused has since moved out.
A rented accommodation, government quarters, or any dwelling — not just owned property — where the accused and child cohabited in a domestic relationship.
A home where the accused lives as a live-in partner of the child's parent, thereby forming a domestic relationship with the child through that parent.
A foster care home where the foster parent and child reside together, as foster care is recognised under the domestic relationship definition.
what_it_excludes: A household where the accused has no domestic relationship with the child, such as a neighbour's house or a stranger's dwelling, even if the accused has visited it frequently.

Institutional premises like hostels, schools, jails, or hospitals — even if the accused and child both reside there — as these are not 'domestic relationship' households in the personal/familial sense.
A household where the accused merely visited the child without ever residing there, as transient presence without cohabitation does not satisfy the 'lives or has lived' requirement.

A household shared solely due to a professional or employment relationship, such as a domestic worker living on the premises, where no domestic relationship as defined under the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 exists.
Cases where the accused and child live in entirely separate households with no history of cohabitation, regardless of any biological or legal relationship between them.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a location qualifies as a 'shared household' is decisive in determining whether a penetrative sexual assault or sexual assault is classified as 'aggravated' under Sections 5 and 9 of POCSO, which carry significantly higher minimum punishments (up to rigorous imprisonment for life). It directly elevates the severity of the charge and the sentencing exposure for the accused when the offence is committed by someone who lives or has lived in the same household as the child in a domestic relationship.

definitions.definition: "Special Court" means a court designated as such under section 28.
definitions.plain_english: A Special Court is a dedicated court specifically set up by the State Government, in consultation with the Chief Justice of the High Court, to handle cases under the POCSO Act. It is not a regular trial court but a specially designated one whose sole or primary purpose is to try offences of sexual abuse and exploitation of children. This ensures faster and more sensitive handling of cases involving child victims.
real_world_examples: In Mumbai, the Maharashtra government designates a Sessions Court in each district as a Special Court under POCSO, where a judge hears only child sexual abuse cases filed by the Mumbai Police, ensuring the child does not have to wait years in a regular overburdened court queue.

In Delhi, when a school teacher is accused of sexually assaulting a student, the case is directly committed to the designated POCSO Special Court in the district, which conducts a child-friendly trial and ensures the victim's identity is protected throughout the proceedings.

A Special Juvenile Police Unit in Chennai, after registering an FIR for penetrative sexual assault on a minor, reports the matter within 24 hours to the Special Court designated under section 28, which then monitors the progress of the investigation and the child's welfare.

In a rural district of Uttar Pradesh where no standalone Special Court exists, the Court of Session acts as the fallback forum for POCSO cases until a formal Special Court is designated by the State Government under section 28.

The Special Court in Bengaluru exercises its power under section 23 to permit a media house to disclose certain anonymised details about a child victim's background, recording in writing that such disclosure is in the interest of the child's recovery and access to rehabilitative services.

A Special Court in Kolkata, during an in-camera trial of a POCSO case, issues directions to the Special Public Prosecutor regarding the manner of examining the child witness so as to avoid re-traumatisation, exercising its powers under section 35 and 36.
what_it_covers: A court formally designated by the State Government under section 28 of POCSO in consultation with the Chief Justice of the High Court, specifically to try offences under the Act.
The court competent to grant permission under section 23 for media disclosure of a child's identity when it is in the interest of the child.
The court to which the Special Juvenile Police Unit or local police must report the matter within 24 hours of receiving information about an offence, as required under section 19(6).
The court that has the power to take cognizance of offences under POCSO, conduct trials, record evidence of the child, and pass orders for care and protection of the child during and after trial.
The court before which the Special Public Prosecutor appointed under section 32 appears to conduct cases on behalf of the State.
what_it_excludes: Regular criminal courts such as a Judicial Magistrate's Court or Chief Metropolitan Magistrate's Court that have not been specifically designated under section 28, even if they handle criminal matters.

Family Courts, Juvenile Justice Boards, or Child Welfare Committees, which are separate statutory bodies and do not qualify as a Special Court under POCSO even though they deal with child-related matters.

The Court of Session acting in its ordinary capacity before any formal designation under section 28 — it serves only as a fallback forum where no Special Court has been designated, not as a Special Court per se.
High Courts or the Supreme Court of India, which exercise appellate or supervisory jurisdiction and are not 'designated' as Special Courts under section 28.
Any tribunal, arbitral body, or quasi-judicial authority, regardless of how specialised, as the definition strictly refers to a court designated through the statutory process under section 28.
definitions.why_it_matters: The designation of a court as a 'Special Court' determines which forum has exclusive jurisdiction to try offences under POCSO, triggering the application of child-sensitive procedural safeguards such as in-camera trials, time-bound proceedings, and the appointment of a Special Public Prosecutor; cases filed before any non-designated court would not benefit from these protections and could be challenged on jurisdictional grounds. Reporting obligations under sections 19 and 34, media restrictions under section 23, and the entire trial framework under sections 28–38 are operative only in relation to this designated court.

definitions.definition: A special educator, as used under this Act, is a person having requisite qualifications and experience in communicating with or educating children who have a mental or physical disability, engaged by the Magistrate, police officer, or Special Court to assist in recording the statement or evidence of such a child, on payment of fees as may be prescribed by the Central Government.
definitions.plain_english: A special educator is a trained professional who knows how to communicate with children who have physical or mental disabilities. When a child with such a disability is a victim or witness in a sexual offence case under this Act, the police, magistrate, or court can call upon this expert to help the child express themselves clearly during statement recording or court proceedings. The government sets the qualifications, experience requirements, and payment for such a person.
real_world_examples: A 9-year-old deaf-mute girl from Lucknow who has been sexually assaulted cannot communicate verbally. The police officer recording her statement engages a certified special educator trained in Indian Sign Language to assist in accurately capturing her account of the incident.

A 12-year-old boy with moderate intellectual disability from Mumbai is a victim of penetrative sexual assault. During the Special Court trial, the judge appoints a special educator experienced in working with children with intellectual disabilities to help translate the child's responses into understandable testimony.

A 7-year-old child with autism spectrum disorder from Bengaluru, who is a witness to a sexual offence committed against a sibling, is brought before a Magistrate. The Magistrate summons a certified special educator familiar with augmentative and alternative communication (AAC) tools to facilitate the child's statement recording.

A 10-year-old girl with cerebral palsy and limited speech from Kolkata reports sexual harassment at her school. The police officer, unable to understand her communication, seeks the assistance of a government-empanelled special educator from a nearby rehabilitation centre to record her statement accurately under Section 26.

A 13-year-old visually impaired child with an additional learning disability from Chennai needs to record evidence before the Special Court. The court engages a special educator who uses Braille-based communication and tactile methods to help the child articulate evidence in a manner admissible before the court.
what_it_covers: A certified professional trained in special education with qualifications prescribed by the Central Government under the rules framed under this Act, engaged to assist in recording a disabled child's statement or evidence.

A special educator working with children having physical disabilities such as deafness, mutism, blindness, or cerebral palsy who cannot communicate in a standard verbal manner during police or magisterial proceedings.

A special educator experienced in communicating with children with mental disabilities such as intellectual disability, autism spectrum disorder, or other cognitive impairments, helping authorities accurately record such a child's statement or court evidence.

Any person formally appointed by a police officer, Magistrate, or Special Court under Sections 26 or 38 to bridge the communication gap between the child victim/witness and the legal authority, within the framework of prescribed qualifications and fee structures.
what_it_excludes: A general schoolteacher or tutor without formal special education training or the qualifications prescribed under the Act's rules, even if personally familiar with the child.

A translator or interpreter engaged under the same sections solely to address language barriers in cases where the child does not have a mental or physical disability — these are distinct roles covered separately in Sections 26 and 38.

A parent, guardian, or trusted adult accompanying the child under Section 26(1), as their role is to provide emotional support and confidence to the child, not to assist in communication due to disability.

Medical professionals such as psychologists or psychiatrists who may examine or treat the child, as their engagement is governed by provisions relating to medical examination and treatment rather than the special educator role under Sections 26 and 38.
definitions.why_it_matters: The engagement of a special educator is a procedural safeguard that ensures the statement or evidence of a child with mental or physical disability is validly and accurately recorded under Sections 26 and 38; failure to use such assistance where necessary could compromise the evidentiary value of the child's statement and undermine the prosecution of the offence. It also triggers a fee obligation and qualification standard mandated by rules framed by the Central Government under Section 45.

definitions.definition: The Special Juvenile Police Unit means a unit of police designated for handling matters relating to children under the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2000, and equipped to receive reports of offences committed or likely to be committed against children under this Act, take immediate protective action, and coordinate with the Child Welfare Committee and Special Court within twenty-four hours of receiving such a report.
definitions.plain_english: A Special Juvenile Police Unit (SJPU) is a dedicated police unit trained specifically to handle cases involving children. When someone reports that a child has been sexually abused or is in danger of being abused, this unit receives the complaint, records it properly, and must arrange care and protection for the child within 24 hours. It also informs the Child Welfare Committee and the Special Court about the case without unnecessary delay.
real_world_examples: A teacher in Pune notices signs of sexual abuse on a student and calls the local SJPU, which records the complaint, arranges for the child to be taken to a government hospital for medical examination, and notifies the Child Welfare Committee the same day.

A hotel staff member in Mumbai discovers a video clip on a guest's laptop that appears to be child pornography; he reports the material to the SJPU, which registers the complaint and initiates action under Sections 13 and 14 of POCSO.

A neighbour in Delhi overhears a child being sexually assaulted in the adjoining flat and informs the SJPU; the unit records the report in a simple language the child understands, arranges a translator for a child who speaks only Bengali, and admits the child to a shelter home within 24 hours.

A photography studio owner in Chennai notices that a customer repeatedly brings a minor for obscene photo shoots; the studio owner reports this to the SJPU, which registers the information, seizes the material, and reports the matter to the Special Court.

A social worker in Kolkata receives a tip-off that a group of children are being exploited for pornographic content; she reports it to the SJPU, which coordinates with the Child Welfare Committee to remove the children from danger and initiates criminal proceedings before the Special Court.
what_it_covers: A designated police unit empowered to receive reports of offences under POCSO from any person, including the child victim herself or himself.
The authority to make immediate arrangements for care and protection of a child in need, including admitting the child to a shelter home or nearest hospital within 24 hours of receiving a report.
The obligation to report the matter to the Child Welfare Committee and the Special Court (or Court of Session where no Special Court is designated) without unnecessary delay and within 24 hours.
The duty to record reports from child informants in simple language, and to provide a translator or interpreter where the child does not understand the language being used.
Reception of information from media personnel, hotel staff, studio operators, or photographic facility workers who come across sexually exploitative material involving children under Section 20.
what_it_excludes: General police stations or officers not specifically designated as a Special Juvenile Police Unit, even though local police are independently empowered to receive the same reports under Section 19.
Civilian bodies such as NGOs, Child Welfare Committees, or school authorities, which may assist in child protection but do not constitute an SJPU and do not carry its statutory obligations.
Courts, prosecutors, or judicial officers, who operate downstream in the criminal process and are distinct from the law-enforcement intake function performed by the SJPU.
Private security agencies or corporate compliance officers, who have no statutory recognition as an SJPU regardless of their involvement in detecting child abuse incidents.

The National Commission for Protection of Child Rights (NCPCR) or State Commissions, which are regulatory and monitoring bodies and are not vested with the first-response investigative functions of an SJPU.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a report is made to the Special Juvenile Police Unit triggers a strict set of statutory obligations — entry numbering, written recording, 24-hour care and protection arrangement, and mandatory intimation to the Child Welfare Committee and Special Court — the failure of which can attract liability for the officer in default. The SJPU's involvement also activates the child-sensitive procedural protections under POCSO, such as recording statements in simple language and providing interpreters, which directly affect the admissibility and reliability of evidence in proceedings before the Special Court.

definitions.definition: 'Special Public Prosecutor' means a Public Prosecutor appointed under section 32, being a person notified by the State Government in the Official Gazette to conduct cases exclusively under the provisions of this Act before every Special Court, provided such person has been in practice as an advocate for not less than seven years.
definitions.plain_english: A Special Public Prosecutor is a senior lawyer with at least seven years of experience who is officially appointed by the State Government specifically to argue cases under the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act in the designated Special Court. Unlike a regular public prosecutor who handles general criminal cases, this person works exclusively on child sexual offence cases. Once appointed, they are treated as a Public Prosecutor under the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973.
real_world_examples: In Mumbai, the Maharashtra State Government issues a Gazette notification appointing an advocate with 10 years of practice as the Special Public Prosecutor for the POCSO Special Court in the City Civil and Sessions Court complex, empowering her to solely handle all POCSO trials in that court.

Following a high-profile case of aggravated penetrative sexual assault on a minor in Delhi, the Delhi Government appoints a senior advocate with over 15 years of criminal law experience as Special Public Prosecutor to ensure dedicated and expert prosecution of the accused before the designated Special Court.

In a district in Uttar Pradesh, the State Government appoints a local advocate with eight years of practice as the Special Public Prosecutor for the POCSO Special Court in Lucknow, who then appears on behalf of the State to record the examination-in-chief of a child victim by communicating questions through the Special Court.

In Tamil Nadu, after the creation of additional POCSO Special Courts under a court expansion drive, the State Government notifies through the Official Gazette the appointment of three different Special Public Prosecutors, each assigned to one of the newly established Special Courts across Chennai, Madurai, and Coimbatore.

In Rajasthan, a Special Public Prosecutor appointed under POCSO requests the Special Court to award compensation to a child survivor for psychological trauma suffered, exercising powers under Section 33 to seek rehabilitation-directed relief in addition to criminal punishment of the offender.
what_it_covers: An advocate with at least seven years of practice appointed by the State Government via Official Gazette notification to conduct all cases under POCSO before a designated Special Court.

A person who, upon appointment, is deemed to be a Public Prosecutor within the meaning of clause (u) of section 2 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, and to whom all provisions of that Code apply accordingly.

The Special Public Prosecutor's role in conducting examination-in-chief, cross-examination, and re-examination of child witnesses by communicating questions through the Special Court under Section 33.

Prosecution of offences including penetrative sexual assault, aggravated penetrative sexual assault, sexual assault, aggravated sexual assault, sexual harassment, and child pornography offences exclusively under POCSO.
what_it_excludes: A regular Public Prosecutor or Additional Public Prosecutor appointed under the Code of Criminal Procedure for general Sessions Court trials who has not been specifically notified under Section 32 of POCSO.
An advocate with less than seven years of practice, regardless of their expertise or willingness, as they do not meet the minimum eligibility threshold prescribed under Section 32(2).
A Private Counsel or defense lawyer engaged by the accused, even if the accused's counsel appears before the Special Court alongside the Special Public Prosecutor.

A Central Government-appointed prosecutor or a prosecutor appointed by any authority other than the State Government, as the appointment power under Section 32 vests exclusively in the State Government.
definitions.why_it_matters: The appointment of a Special Public Prosecutor is a procedural prerequisite for the effective functioning of the Special Court under POCSO, as only this officer can conduct the State's case against the accused; without a validly appointed Special Public Prosecutor, the conduct of trial, recording of child testimony through the court, and seeking of compensation under Section 33 may be procedurally compromised. The designation also ensures that a person deemed a Public Prosecutor under CrPC carries all attendant rights, duties, and powers during POCSO proceedings, directly affecting the validity of prosecution acts and the child victim's right to protected, child-friendly trial procedures.

Covers: An advocate with at least seven years of practice appointed by the State Government via Official Gazette notification to conduct all cases under POCSO before a designated Special Court.; A person who, upon appointment, is deemed to be a Public Prosecutor within the meaning of clause (u) of section 2 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, and to whom all provisions of that Code apply accordingly.; The Special Public Prosecutor's role in conducting examination-in-chief, cross-examination, and re-examination of child witnesses by communicating questions through the Special Court under Section 33.; Prosecution of offences including penetrative sexual assault, aggravated penetrative sexual assault, sexual assault, aggravated sexual assault, sexual harassment, and child pornography offences exclusively under POCSO.

Excludes: A regular Public Prosecutor or Additional Public Prosecutor appointed under the Code of Criminal Procedure for general Sessions Court trials who has not been specifically notified under Section 32 of POCSO.; An advocate with less than seven years of practice, regardless of their expertise or willingness, as they do not meet the minimum eligibility threshold prescribed under Section 32(2).; A Private Counsel or defense lawyer engaged by the accused, even if the accused's counsel appears before the Special Court alongside the Special Public Prosecutor.; A Central Government-appointed prosecutor or a prosecutor appointed by any authority other than the State Government, as the appointment power under Section 32 vests exclusively in the State Government.

Why it matters: The appointment of a Special Public Prosecutor is a procedural prerequisite for the effective functioning of the Special Court under POCSO, as only this officer can conduct the State's case against the accused; without a validly appointed Special Public Prosecutor, the conduct of trial, recording of child testimony through the court, and seeking of compensation under Section 33 may be procedurally compromised. The designation also ensures that a person deemed a Public Prosecutor under CrPC carries all attendant rights, duties, and powers during POCSO proceedings, directly affecting the validity of prosecution acts and the child victim's right to protected, child-friendly trial procedures.

(Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012)

definitions.law_name: Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012
definitions.definition: For the purposes of Section 13, the expression 'use a child' shall include involving a child through any medium like print, electronic, computer or any other technology for preparation, production, offering, transmitting, publishing, facilitation and distribution of the pornographic material.
definitions.plain_english: Using a child means involving a minor in any way — through print, internet, television, computers, or any other technology — to create, make available, send, publish, or share sexual or pornographic material. It does not matter whether the material is kept privately or distributed publicly. The term covers every step of the process, from preparing and producing such material to sharing or facilitating access to it.
real_world_examples: A photographer in Mumbai photographs a minor child in a sexually explicit pose and uploads the images to a private WhatsApp group — this constitutes 'using a child' at the production and distribution stages.

A cable TV operator in Delhi broadcasts an advertisement featuring a child in an indecent or obscene manner for commercial purposes — this amounts to using a child through the electronic medium of television.

A person in Bengaluru uses editing software on a personal laptop to prepare digital pornographic content featuring a child and stores it on a hard drive even without sharing it — the preparation stage alone qualifies as using a child.

A social media influencer in Chennai facilitates the transmission of child sexual abuse material (CSAM) by forwarding a link containing such content through Telegram — the act of facilitation and transmitting covers 'use a child' under this section.

A printing press operator in Kolkata prints magazines containing obscene representations of children and hands them over for distribution — involvement in the print medium at the preparation and distribution stage constitutes using a child.

An adult in Hyderabad coerces a minor to perform simulated sexual acts on a webcam for a live-streamed online session — the use of computer and internet technology for real-time transmission falls squarely within this definition.
what_it_covers: Involving a child in the preparation or production of pornographic material through any technology, including cameras, computers, or mobile phones.
Transmitting, publishing, or distributing content featuring a child for purposes of sexual gratification via the internet, electronic platforms, or print media.
Facilitating the creation or spread of child pornography by providing infrastructure, platforms, or technical assistance, even without directly appearing in the material.
Using a child in television programmes, online advertisements, or digital content that constitutes an indecent or obscene representation of the child.
Offering or making available child pornographic material through any digital or physical medium, regardless of whether it is intended for personal use or wider distribution.
what_it_excludes: Medical or scientific documentation of a child's anatomy created strictly for legitimate clinical, educational, or forensic purposes with proper authorisation and no sexual gratification intent.
Age-appropriate artistic or creative depictions of children in mainstream cinema, theatre, or literature that do not amount to indecent, obscene, or sexually explicit representation.

Purely verbal or written description of child sexual abuse in a legal case record, investigative report, or academic research paper that does not involve the child being photographed, filmed, or otherwise materially used.

Actions by a child who is themselves a victim and has not been 'involved' voluntarily or involuntarily by any other person — the definition targets the person who involves or exploits the child, not the child.
Content involving adults that is falsely or mistakenly labelled as involving children, where no actual child has been used in the preparation, production, or distribution process.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act qualifies as 'use a child' under Section 13 directly determines whether an accused is liable for the offence of using a child for pornographic purposes, which is punishable under Section 14 of POCSO with rigorous imprisonment. A broader interpretation of this term — encompassing preparation, facilitation, and distribution — ensures that every participant in the chain of child sexual abuse material production faces criminal liability, not just those who directly film or photograph the child.
